summary: The 1851 treaty recognized a Cheyenne and Arapaho territory bounded by the North Platte, the Rocky Mountain main range, the Arkansas to the Santa Fe road crossing, and a line to the Platte forks. Tribes kept hunting, fishing and passage rights over other tracts and did not abandon claims to other lands.

citation: Statutes at Large vol. 11, note "Treaty of Fort Laramie"; 11 Stat. 749 (explanatory note)

summary: The Senate amended the 1851 treaty in 1852 (Kappler prints the amended annuity term: $50,000 a year for ten years, plus up to five more at the President's discretion). The amendments needed tribal assent, and the official Statutes note says the assent of all the tribes had not been obtained, so the treaty was never proclaimed or printed, though Congress appropriated money under it. Kappler's headnote calls it "never ratified or printed." Status: Senate-amended, never completed or proclaimed. Neither "ratified" nor "never ratified" alone is accurate.

That Arapahos and Cheyennes regarded the spoken council as the real treaty is the characterization of Fowler 2015:366 and Roberts 1984:65-66, not a fact from the record. The 1864 Camp Weld record shows White Antelope asking "How can we be protected from the soldiers on the plains?" (S. summary: Article 4 made tribes liable for 'depredations' while Article 8 let the President withhold annuities; there was no mechanism for tribes to enforce US violations, and promised protection never came.

citation: Kansas-Nebraska Act, May 30, 1854, sec. 19 (Kansas proviso); 10 Stat. 277, sec. 19
quote: or to include any territory which, by treaty with any Indian tribe, is not, without the consent of said tribe, to be included within the territorial limits or jurisdiction of any State or Territory
summary: The Kansas-Nebraska Act did not exclude all Indian lands from Kansas Territory. It excluded only land that a treaty said could not be put in a territory without the tribe's consent, and it otherwise preserved Indian rights of person and property until extinguished by treaty. The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty has no such non-inclusion clause, so the Cheyenne-Arapaho land lay inside Kansas Territory's boundaries, but Indian title to it had not been extinguished. Creating Arapahoe County and opening it to settlement in 1855 ran against unextinguished Indian title and the 1834 Act, not against an exclusion from the territory.

instrument: 4 Stat. 729 secs. 10-11 (1834 Act); 5 Stat. 657 (1844 Townsite Act); 13 Stat. 94 (1864 Denver act); 12 Stat. 1163 (Fort Wise)

quote: was originally laid out by a company or association of persons, on the public domain of the United States, before the same had been
summary: Gold-rush town companies laid out Denver, Auraria and other towns in 1858-59, and Boulder in 1859, on land the 1851 treaty recognized as Cheyenne and Arapaho and that no treaty had yet ceded. The 1844 Townsite Act (5 Stat. 657) applied only to surveyed public lands, so it gave the town companies no title. Denver occupants got a path to title only through a special act of May 28, 1864 (13 Stat. 94), after Fort Wise; the probate judge entered the site on May 6, 1865. In 1873 the Supreme Court described the site as laid out "on the public domain" before survey: that is the federal view, written after the cessions. The 100,000 trespasser figure and the claim that no one was fined or removed under the 1834 Act were not verified.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861, 12 Stat. 1163 (Art. 11 struck by Senate Aug. 6, 1861; assent dated [Oct. 29, 1861], 12 Stat. 1168); Kappler II 807
citation: William E. Unrau, "A Prelude to War," Colorado Magazine 41(4) (1964); Unrau 1964:300, citing Greenwood to Thompson, Oct. 25, 1860, ARCIA 1860 pp. 452-454
quote: Only a few tribal leaders with questionable authority
summary: Greenwood stayed at Fort Wise only twelve days (Unrau 1964:300). Unrau says a few leaders "with questionable authority made verbal promises" to cede land for annuities and a reservation, while Greenwood reported measurable success; the Northern Cheyennes and Arapahoes were absent. The claim that the leaders "refused his treaty" is not supported: Unrau describes verbal promises, not a refusal. The names Black Kettle, White Antelope, Little Raven, Left Hand are not in Unrau. The ICC (10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, Finding 36) confirms only the Southern bands were parties to the 1861 treaty.

instrument: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807

quote: Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head, and Big Mouth, (on the part of the Arapahoes,) and Black Kettle, White Antelope, Lean Bear, Little Wolf, Tall Bear, and Left Hand, or Namos, (on the part of the Cheyennes,)
summary: The treaty was made by commissioners A. G. Boone and F. B. Culver, not by Boone alone. The four Arapaho marks were Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head and Big Mouth, all Southern. No Northern Arapaho signed. A "Left Hand, or Namos" signed on the Cheyenne side; he is a Cheyenne, not the Arapaho Left Hand (Niwot), who did not sign. The same ten men signed the assent to the Senate amendment on Oct. 29, 1861. The text says the signers were "duly authorized" by the confederated tribes; the claim that they said they spoke only for their own bands is from Roberts 1984 and Fowler 2015, not the treaty.

summary: The starvation threat is the account of Cheyenne and Arapaho descendants in the History Colorado Sand Creek exhibition text (2022-2023); label it as their account. The written record is silent on threats, and Commissioner Dole reported the amendment assent was "readily given". Independent support for hunger: Unrau (1964:303) writes that on Feb. 18, 1861 Boone and Culver "issued supplies to the starving Indians in exchange for" marks on the treaty, which supports PSL's statement that provisions were used to induce signatures.

quote: Sandy Fork of the Arkansas River and extending westwardly along the said river to the mouth of Purgatory River
summary: Fort Wise reserved a tract from the mouth of Sandy Fork west along the Arkansas to the Purgatoire, up the Purgatoire to New Mexico's north line, west to a line due south of a point 5 miles east of the Huerfano mouth, then north to beginning. Eastern part to the Arapaho. It was dry, far from bison; promised houses, mill and tools never came, and agent Colley leased part to whites.

instrument: 12 Stat. 1163 (Fort Wise); 15 Stat. 655 Art. 2 (1868 Northern cession); 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1
citation: ICC findings of fact on value, Cheyenne-Arapaho, Dockets 329 and 348 (Dec. 6, 1961); 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, finding 36
quote: officials of the Government were unsuccessful in securing a treaty of cession from them cntil the Treaty of May 10, 1868
summary: The federal record itself shows that Fort Wise did not settle the northern lands. Commissioner Dole's 1863 report says many bands were left out at Fort Wise and still claimed their right to the country had never been relinquished. Evans sought a further agreement in 1863 to get "an undoubted cession". The 1865 Little Arkansas treaty records the tribes' claim never to have relinquished title. The Indian Claims Commission found that only Southern bands were parties to Fort Wise and that the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho ceded only by the treaty of May 10, 1868 (15 Stat. 655, Art. 2). Show the land north of the South Platte as not ceded by its occupants from 1861 to 1868. Browne's 1862-63 opinion was not seen and rests on Unrau 1964.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861, 12 Stat. 1163 (Art. 11 struck by Senate Aug. 6, 1861; assent dated [Oct. 29, 1861], 12 Stat. 1168); Kappler II 807
citation: Unrau, "A Prelude to War," Colorado Magazine 41(4) (1964); Unrau 1964:309, 311
quote: Dole's letter of retraction to Evans was a wordy, ambiguous
summary: Dole did reverse his earlier ruling (that lands north of the South Platte were not ceded) in a letter Unrau calls "wordy, ambiguous", telling Evans the 1861 treaty ceded all lands not claimed by the treaty bands (Unrau 1964:311). But "defiance of federal law and recognition of the whole affair as a fait accompli" is, in Unrau (p. 309), one of three alternatives facing the agents after Article VI expired Dec. 6, 1862, not a finding that the US chose it. Unrau says the agents then cast their lot with the settlers.

instrument: Proposed Northern Arapaho reserve; Evans order to Maj. Loree
citation: Upper Platte agreement of Aug. 19, 1863, with Loree certificate (ARCIA 1863); ARCIA 1863, Colorado Superintendency, pp. 131-132 (doc. No. 54)
quote: not to deliver their annuity goods to them until after the time appointed for the council with them
summary: On Aug. 19, 1863, at the Upper Platte agency, the Arapaho chiefs Black Bear, Roman Nose and Friday and the Cheyennes Spotted Horse and Shield made their marks on an agreement to abide by Fort Wise. Agent Loree certified he had told them his instructions were not to hand out annuity goods until after the council, and the paper states the annuities were distributed "in consideration of" the agreement. The withholding came from Loree's instructions for the treaty commission (Evans, Loree, Colley); the paper does not show a direct Evans order to withhold food. In July 1864 agent Whitely reported that Friday wanted a reserve on the north bank of the Cache la Poudre, from Box Elder Creek to the Platte and north to Crow Creek. That would have displaced about sixteen white families, and no reserve was made.

instrument: RIT 315 (NARA, as cited by PSL); atlas: 12 Stat. 1163, Kappler II:807
citation: Statement of Robert Bent, in Condition of the Indian Tribes (Doolittle report); S. Rep. No. 156, 39th Cong., 2d Sess. (1867), App. 96
quote: I have heard the Indians charge Major Colley with trading their own goods to them.
summary: Contemporaries accused agent Samuel G. Colley of diverting Arapaho and Cheyenne annuity goods. Robert Bent swore that goods being traded in the Sand Creek camp were "said to belong to Dexter Colley [the agent's son] and John Smith" and that Indians charged Colley with trading their own goods to them. Present this as a documented contemporaneous accusation, not a proven theft. That Colley was Dole's cousin rests on Unrau 1964:304 ("Dear Cousin William" letters), not checked here. The $3,000 from Evans was not verified.

citation: Evans to Colley, Sept. 29, 1864 (ARCIA 1864); ARCIA 1864, Colorado Superintendency, p. 220
quote: I have declined to make any treaty with them lest it might embarrass the military operations
summary: At Camp Weld Evans refused to make peace with Arapaho and Cheyenne leaders and later wrote that his talk offered them nothing; Chivington's assurance that those surrendering to Wynkoop were not hostile 'turned out to be a lie'.

citation: Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War, Massacre of Cheyenne Indians (1865), report; JCCW, 38th Cong., 2d Sess. (1865), Massacre of Cheyenne Indians, p. iii
quote: from 8 to 10 lodges of Arapahoes under Left Hand
summary: At Sand Creek on Nov. 29, 1864, Chivington's troops attacked a camp of about 100 Cheyenne lodges and 8 to 10 Arapaho lodges under Left Hand (Niwot). The JCCW report found these Indians friendly and the attack a deliberate massacre. Left Hand's death there, or soon after from wounds, comes from scholarly sources, not this report. "Genocide" is PSL's characterization.

citation: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862, secs. 2-3; 12 Stat. 489, 491-492, secs. 2-3
quote: to the amount of five alternate sections per mile on each side of said railroad
summary: The 1862 Pacific Railway Act told the US to "extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles" along the line, and it granted five alternate sections per mile on each side (ten sections, 6,400 acres, per mile), mineral lands excepted. "Ten square miles on each side" matches the 1864 amendment, which doubled the grant; that amendment was not checked here. That the two 1862 acts took homelands without tribal consent is the descendants' characterization (History Colorado exhibit). Evans's railroad grants were not verified.

instrument: ICC Docket 329-D (Northern Arapaho), 12 Ind. Cl. Comm. 212 (1963): compromise settlement $3,230,000; value findings 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 (1961)
citation: Indian Claims Commission Final Report (1978), alphabetical index of cases; ICC Docket 329-D, 12 Ind. Cl. Comm. 212 (June 27, 1963)
quote: Findings - Compromise settlement 6/27/63 $3,230,000.00
summary: Northern Arapaho TREC recommendations ask Colorado to support reopening the ICC settlement, calling valuations biased and the final award 'unscrupulous and dishonorable', and questioning the 'unratified' 1851 treaty and the Fort Wise taking.

citation: Testimony of Gov. John Evans, Condition of the Indian Tribes (Doolittle report); S. Rep. No. 156, 39th Cong., 2d Sess. (1867), App. 45-46
quote: He said the white people had taken their gold and their lands
summary: Northern Arapaho leaders said in 1863 that whites had taken their gold and lands, and that they had not been at Fort Wise (Little Owl, reported by Evans). The ICC found that the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho did not cede until the treaty of May 10, 1868. Gold mining from 1858 to 1868 therefore took place on land its northern occupants had not ceded. But the 1868 treaty (15 Stat. 655, Art. 2) relinquished all territory outside the reservations it named, and in 1963 the ICC paid the Northern Arapaho $3,230,000 in a compromise of the land claim (Docket 329-D). "Never signed a treaty and ceded" is accurate for 1858-1868 but not as a statement about the land today. Water rights were not checked.

quote: The forced removal was an act of genocide.
summary: The tribe calls its forced removal from Colorado an act of genocide tied to Evans, and seeks compensation, restored hunting/gathering rights on public lands, return of abandoned railroad land, GOCO access, tax relief, and tuition waivers; it notes the State School Fund received 4 million acres and CSU still holds 19,000 acres of Arapaho land.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 177
quote: the necessity of extinguishing the Indians’ title
summary: Drunken miners attacked Left Hand's village on Cherry Creek while the men were away, raping women and stealing horses; the Rocky Mountain News used it to argue for extinguishing Indian title.

quote: Congress has not thought it necessary to make any new definition of Indian country.
summary: The 1834 Act defined Indian country, let agents remove intruders, and fined anyone settling on land "belonging, secured, or granted by treaty" to a tribe $1,000. It did not declare Cheyenne title as such, and it did not bar all non-traders: it licensed traders and required passports of foreigners. The federal government did not remove the gold-rush settlers. The Act was not "rescinded in 1873": in 1877 the Supreme Court (Bates v. Clark) still applied its definition of Indian country. Linking non-enforcement to Sand Creek is TREC's argument.

citation: TREC pp. 240-241, quoting Jefferson Davis via a secondary work; TREC 2024 pp. 240-241
quote: In every treaty we evaluated, the process was the same. Treaty commissioners represented the United States government; most often, these
summary: The source says 'treaty negotiations are a myth': commissioners arrived with prepared texts, read articles aloud, heard objections, and sent the unchanged text to the Senate, while Native leaders believed their spoken input was incorporated. Lakota speak of the 'Chicago Re-write' for 1868.

instrument: Cheyenne governance: Council of Forty-Four Chiefs
citation: Sheldon Spotted Elk (2012 law review article) as quoted by TREC pp. 241-244; TREC 2024 pp. 241-244
quote: The Council of Forty-Four Chiefs was a self-perpetuating body of tribal trustees; each member was selected by a predecessor
summary: Cheyenne national decisions, especially war and peace and treaties, belonged to the Council of 44 (ten-year terms, equal band representation, consensus), with military societies (incl. Dog Men / Dog Soldiers) subordinate. This is the standard against which the source judges every treaty signature: individual chiefs acting without Council approval lacked authority.

instrument: Treaty of July 6, 1825, 7 Stat. 255; Kappler II 232 (1904 ed.; p. 164 in the 1903 ed.)
citation: Treaty with the Cheyenne Tribe, July 6, 1825; 7 Stat. 255; Kappler II 232
quote: Ta-ton-ca-pa, or the buffaloe head
summary: First Cheyenne treaty, July 6, 1825, at the mouth of the Teton River: a trade-and-friendship treaty with no land cession. The Cheyenne agreed to give safe conduct to persons authorized by the United States and not to molest Americans travelling to and from New Mexico; it did not open their country to emigrants generally. The signers' names are written in Lakota form (e.g. Ta-ton-ca, Shong-ge-mon-e-to, Oh-kee-che-ta). The Council of 44 approval is TREC's account.

citation: D.D. Mitchell to Commissioner, Nov. 11, 1851, in Kappler IV; Kappler IV 1072
quote: the settling up of all former complaints on the part of the Indians for the destruction of their buffalo, timber, grass, etc., caused by the passage of the whites through their country
summary: Emigrant traffic on the Platte road damaged buffalo, timber and grass, and the 1851 commissioner himself named settling those complaints as a purpose of the treaty. TREC's dating (from about 1845, sharply after 1849) and the word "illegal" for emigrants are TREC's.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851: Kappler IV (1929) 1065-1081 (text, signatures, Indian Office memorandum, Senate Journal); Kappler II 594; 11 Stat. 749 prints only a publisher's note, not the treaty. Senate ratified with amendment May 24, 1852; all eight nations, the Crow last, assented by 1854; never proclaimed; Congress conditioned annuity payment on tribal assent (10 Stat. 238 proviso)
citation: Kappler IV (1929), Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5 and Mitchell report; Kappler IV 1066, Art. 5; 1076
quote: do not surrender the privilege of hunting, fishing, or passing over any of the tracts of country
summary: The speech wording ("We do not want your land") is from Missouri Republican dispatches, not checked. Its substance is in the record: Art. 5 says the nations do not give up claims to other lands or the privilege of hunting, fishing and passing over any tract, and Mitchell's report confirms the promised $50,000 a year for 50 years and that "we have taken, or are rapidly taking away from them all means of support". The Senate cut the term to 10 years (plus 5 at the President's discretion).

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 6, as printed in Kappler IV; Kappler IV 1066 (Art. 6)
quote: having selected principals or head chiefs for their respective nations, through whom all national business will hereafter be conducted, do hereby bind themselves to sustain said chiefs and their successors during good behavior
summary: Article 6 has the nations "having selected" head chiefs and binding themselves to sustain them; the text says the nations selected them, though TREC and historians say the commissioners pushed it. That this subverted Council of 44 governance and set a precedent for collective responsibility is TREC's interpretation.

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 signature list and 1853 Cheyenne-Arapaho assent, in Kappler IV; Kappler IV 1067, 1080
quote: Cheyennes: Wah-ha-nis-satta (his x mark); Voist-ti-toe-vetz (his x mark); Nahk-ko-me-ien (his x mark); Koh-kah-y-wh-cum-est (his x mark).
summary: Four Cheyenne marks are on the 1851 treaty. The assent to the Senate amendment translates them as The Man that Walks Out, White Cow, Old Bark and White Antelope. TREC's list (Stone Forehead, Whiteface Bull, White Antelope, Bear Feather) matches only on White Antelope by name. The band identifications and the claim that no Northern chief signed are TREC's and not shown by the treaty.

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5; Kappler IV 1066; Kappler II 594
quote: The territory of the Cheyennes and Arrapahoes, commencing at the Red Bute, or the place where the road leaves the north fork of the Platte River; thence up the north fork of the Platte River to its source
summary: The US recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as Cheyenne and Arapaho country. The source says assigning two sovereign nations one undivided tract violated their sovereignty and created later confusion; no Cheyenne-Arapaho line was drawn. Article 5 also preserved claims to other lands and hunting, fishing and passage rights.

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5; Agreement of 1876 ratified Feb. 28, 1877, Art. 1; Kappler IV 1066; 19 Stat. 254, Art. 1
quote: relinquish and cede to the United States all the territory lying outside
summary: Article 5 did keep the privilege of hunting, fishing and passing over the described tracts. Whether those privileges survive is TREC's argument. Later instruments signed by Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho leaders reached them: the May 10, 1868 treaty kept only a right to roam and hunt while game lasted, and the 1876 agreement (ratified 1877) ceded all territory outside the Sioux reservation "including all privileges of hunting".

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Arts. 3-4; Act of June 30, 1834, sec. 11; Kappler IV 1065-1066; 4 Stat. 729, sec. 11
quote: whilst lawfully residing in or passing through their respective territories
summary: Article 3 bound the US to protect the nations against depredations by US citizens but named no enforcement method; the 1834 Act's settler penalty was $1,000 (sec. 11) and removal (sec. 10), and was not used against the gold-rush settlers. TREC's claim that "lawfully residing" conflicts with the 1834 Act is overstated: licensed traders, agents and their employees could lawfully reside in Indian country.

summary: Article 8 let the President withhold annuities from a whole nation for violations by any member, with no due process; the source calls it collective punishment and says the government did later manipulate annuities.

quote: The Indians appear to have construed their signature to the paper forwarded by Major Wynkoop as only a general consent of friendship with the whites, but not as surrendering the Smoky Hill country.
summary: In Feb.-Mar. 1866 Wynkoop distributed goods and then had Medicine Arrows, Big Head and other Dog Soldier leaders sign a paper binding them to the 1865 treaty; the escort officer told them he would "enforce the treaty to the letter", and Big Head objected to the Smoky Hill route. The Commissioner himself reported that the signers understood it as a pledge of friendship, not a surrender of the Smoky Hill country. "Bribing" and "threatening" are Berthrong's characterizations. The Leavenworth complaint was not checked.

citation: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas), Senate amendment and assent; 14 Stat. 708-709 (Senate resolution May 22, 1866; assent at Fort Zarah Nov. 10, 1866)
quote: shall designate for said tribes a reservation, no part of which shall be within the State of Kansas
summary: Under pressure from Kansans, the Senate amended the treaty so the reservation could include no land in Kansas. Black Kettle and Little Robe signed the amended treaty in Nov 1866, but the Dog Soldiers and many Southern Cheyennes did not recognize it; Black Kettle had already repudiated the Smoky Hill cession.

citation: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, 1868; Peace Commission Report 1868, pp. 10-11
quote: he at once ordered the Indian village, of about three hundred lodges together with the entire property of the tribes, to be burned.
summary: Hancock marched cavalry, infantry and artillery toward a Cheyenne-Sioux village on Pawnee Fork in April 1867; the people fled, fearing another Sand Creek, and Hancock ordered the village of about 300 lodges burned after news that fleeing Indians had attacked a Smoky Hill station. The Peace Commission said this made "the Indian ... an outlaw" on the plains. The 1,400-troop figure, the April 19 date and the Sherman "coaxed out ... or killed" quote are from Berthrong and were not checked.

citation: Act of July 20, 1867, ch. 32 (Indian Peace Commission act); 15 Stat. 17, sec. 5
quote: not exceeding four thousand men in number, and for such term of service as, in his judgment, may be necessary for the suppression of Indian hostilities.
summary: The act said that if the commissioners failed to secure the Indians' consent to remove to reservations and failed to secure peace, the Secretary of War could accept up to 4,000 mounted volunteers "for the suppression of Indian hostilities". The act authorized this; it did not order it, and it does not use the words "force onto reservations".

citation: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge); Commissioner Parker to Secretary Cox, Aug. 10, 1869; 15 Stat. 597-598 (signatures); Kappler I (1904) 841
quote: TALL BULL
summary: Fourteen Cheyennes (including Bull Bear, Tall Bull and White Horse of the Dog Soldiers, and Black Kettle) and eight Arapahos signed. Roman Nose did not sign. In 1869 the Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported that the tribes "did not understand the location of the reservation" and had never been on it. That gifts and destitution motivated signing is the Colorado Encyclopedia's inference.

citation: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge); 15 Stat. 596, Arts. X-XI; 15 Stat. 594, Art. II
quote: on any lands south of the Arkansas so long as the buffalo may range
summary: The treaty created a reservation just south of the Kansas border, reserved hunting on any lands south of the Arkansas while buffalo ranged, barred white settlement on the old 1865 reservation for three years, and promised agent, physician, schools, implements and 30 years of annuities. Source says it was never adhered to in its original terms; no reservation was established in 1868.

citation: NPS, "What Happened to the Bison?"; nps.gov
quote: the Army provided free ammunition to hide hunters, who brought bison to the brink of extinction
summary: NPS does say this, but NPS is secondary and paraphrases. Do not present it as a direct quotation of the 1873 Interior Secretary. Dodge (1877) gives about 4.37 million killed 1872-74 (3,158,730 by white hunters), not 7.5 million; the 7.5 million figure is Berthrong 1963:381, not checked.

citation: George W. Manypenny, Our Indian Wards (1880); Manypenny 1880, pp. 210-211, 216-217
quote: He had decided on a winter campaign, the objects of which were
summary: Manypenny (former Commissioner of Indian Affairs) wrote that of the $500,000 Congress gave Sherman to carry out the 1867-68 treaties, only $50,000 went to Hazen's southern district, that Sherman sought to stop all goods to the Cheyennes and Arapahos, and that Sheridan stockpiled over a million rations for his winter campaign while feeding the tribes was "the simple performance of an obligation, under the treaties of Medicine Lodge creek". In the pages read he does not say treaty money was diverted to the campaign.

citation: Grinnell, The Fighting Cheyennes (1915), ch. XXIII; Grinnell 1915:301-307
quote: fifty-two Indians, and the capture of eighteen women and chil-
summary: Grinnell, summarizing the military reports, confirms the attack of July 11, 1869 at Summit Springs, fifty-two Indians killed, eighteen women and children captured, and Tall Bull killed in the ravine. That it ended Cheyenne occupation of the Platte-Arkansas country is Berthrong's conclusion (1963:344; lending only). The source calls it a battle; Grinnell notes the reports do not say how many of the dead were women and children.

instrument: Executive order of Aug. 10, 1869, Kappler I (1904) 841
citation: Executive order of Aug. 10, 1869 (Parker recommendation approved by Cox and Grant); Kappler I (1904) 841
quote: did not understand the location of the reservation as defined by the treaty of August 19, 1868; that they have never been upon said reserve, and do not desire to go there
summary: On Aug. 10, 1869 Grant approved the Commissioner's recommendation to locate the Cheyennes and Arapahos on the North Fork of the Canadian. The federal record says this was at the tribes' own request after they had refused the Medicine Lodge reservation. The Commissioner called the land "public land" and said Congress should later confirm a permanent reservation, which it did not do before 1891. ARCIA 1872 put the area at 4,011,500 acres. That this shows treaties were "arbitrary" is the source's argument.

nations: Southern Cheyenne;Southern Arapaho;Wichita and Affiliated Bands
citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, sec. 13, Art. IV; Royce Schedule area 540a; 26 Stat. 1023, Art. IV; Royce 1899 area 540a
quote: in that part thereof now occupied and claimed by the Wichita and affiliated bands of Indians
summary: The Wichita and affiliated bands were assigned part of the Cheyenne-Arapaho executive-order reservation (between the Washita and the Canadian, from the 98th meridian to 98 degrees 40 minutes) under an Oct. 19, 1872 agreement that Congress never ratified. The 1891 act still excluded that area from Cheyenne-Arapaho allotment. The 760,000-acre figure was not checked.

instrument: Unratified Arapaho agreement of 1872 (ARCIA 1872 p. 42); Act of May 29, 1872 authorizing negotiation
citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1872; ARCIA 1872, pp. 42-43
quote: a contract, made subject to the action of Congress, was entered into between the Commissioner of Indian Affairs and the delegation of the Arapaho tribe
summary: In 1872 an Arapaho delegation in Washington signed a contract, subject to Congress, giving up their interest in the Medicine Lodge reservation for a separate reserve; the Commissioner planned "separate negotiations" with the Cheyennes later, so no Cheyennes took part. It was never ratified: the Medicine Lodge reservation was still being ceded in 1891 (26 Stat. 1022, Art. I). The Commissioner claimed the delegation was "fully empowered"; "under pressure" is the source's characterization.

citation: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1883, Cheyenne and Arapaho Agency (Agent Miles); ARCIA 1883, p. 62
quote: At an annual rental of 2 cents per acre, amounting to
summary: Agent Miles reported 1883 grazing leases to seven lessees covering 3,117,880 acres at 2 cents per acre ($62,350.60 a year), not about 2.4 million. The bribery of tribal members and staff, the 426,202-acre restriction, Miles's monopolies and Cleveland's 1885 expulsion rest on Berthrong 1976 and were not checked.

instrument: Attorney contract (10% fee) with tribal chiefs
quote: It was often difficult to determine whose side the attorneys were on.
summary: Former agent Miles and frontier attorneys supposedly representing the tribes held a vague contract, signed deceptively with a tiny group of chiefs, for 10 percent of any settlement; they held secret communications with the commissioners. $67,000 of tribal money went to the attorneys.

instrument: Agreement with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 1890, ratified Act of Mar. 3, 1891, 26 Stat. 989, 1022, ch. 543, sec. 13
citation: 26 Stat. 989, Indian appropriation act Mar. 3, 1891; 26 Stat. 1022-1025, ch. 543, sec. 13
quote: If you don’t do what the President wants you to do, the law of Congress will be put in force
summary: The ratifying act is confirmed (26 Stat. 1022). The Jerome threats, the halved beef ration, and Hagan's judgment about bought signatures are not checked: they need the Cherokee Commission council journal or Hagan 2003:64-65, 79 (lending only). Attribute them to Hagan.

citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890); Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 28, 1867 (Medicine Lodge) Art. XII; 26 Stat. 1022 (sec. 13 preamble); 15 Stat. 597, Art. XII
quote: by Left Hand, his mark, and five hundred and sixty- four others, on the part of the said Indians
summary: Medicine Lodge Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult males to sign any cession of the reservation. The ratified 1891 text records 565 signatures (Left Hand and 564 others). Noble's instruction, Agent Ashley's 618 adult-male count and Berthrong's estimate that about 680 were needed are from Hagan and Berthrong (not checked). The January 1891 protest by seven Cheyenne chiefs was not checked.

citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890); 26 Stat. 1022-1023, Arts. I-II
quote: and all other lands or tracts of country in the Indian Territory to which they have or may set up or allege any right, title, interest or claim whatsoever.
summary: The 1891 agreement ceded the Medicine Lodge reservation tract in the Cherokee Outlet "absolutely" (Art. 1) and the executive-order reservation subject to allotment (Art. 2), plus any other lands they might claim. The words "any rights they might have" are Hagan's paraphrase of Jerome, not the ratified text. Noble's "pay twice" instruction was not checked.

citation: Act of Mar. 3, 1891, ch. 543, sec. 13 (Cheyenne-Arapaho agreement of Oct. 1890); 26 Stat. 1024, Arts. V and VII; 26 Stat. 1025, sec. 15
quote: should any In- dian entitled to allotments hereunder fail or refuse to make his or her selection of land in that time, then the allotting, agent in charge of the work of making such allotments shall
summary: Confirmed: allotting agents assigned allotments to Indians who did not choose within 90 days (Art. 5), and the total price was $1,500,000 (Art. 7). The ratified text gives no per-acre price; "50 cents per acre" and the retained/school/military/opened acreages (Berthrong 1976, 175) were not checked. The same act paid the Choctaw and Chickasaw $2,991,450 for their claimed interest in 2,393,160 acres of the same reservation south of the Canadian (sec. 15).

citation: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861; ICC compromise settlements; 12 Stat. 1163, Art. 1; 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 (1965); 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 (1963)
quote: all the lands now owned, possessed, or claimed by them, wherever situated, except a tract to be reserved for the use of said tribes
summary: Boulder was settled in 1858-59 (not 1851) on land then unceded, inside the 1851 Fort Laramie area. On paper the 1861 Fort Wise treaty then ceded it, and the ICC later paid compromise awards for the 1851 area ($15,000,000 to the Southern tribes in 1965; $4,360,886.19 to the Northern Cheyenne in 1963). "Stolen property, never compensated" is the TREC's position; it is accurate only in the sense that no payment was specific to the site and the tribes reject the 1861 cession.

citation: Indian Claims Commission, Final Report (1978/79), case index; 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 (findings), 185 (opinion), Oct. 18, 1965, Dkts. 329-A and 329-B
quote: Cheyenne and Arapaho 16 162 Findings - Compromise settlement 10/18/65 $15,000,000.. 00
summary: Government offered $15,000,000 to settle all Southern claims, including the claim that $1,500,000 paid for the 1891 taking of 4,608,878 acres was unconscionable. Accepted 338 to 2 at Watonga after notice to 1,542 members. Source argues it was below even the inflation-adjusted 1865 half share ($22.7M) and excluded loss of life and property.

citation: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946, secs. 20(b) and 22; 60 Stat. 1049, 1054-1055, secs. 20(b), 22; 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162
quote: either party may appeal from the determination of the Commission to the Court of Claims
summary: The ICC Act let "either party" appeal a final determination to the Court of Claims, and made payment a "full discharge" of all claims in the controversy. A compromise settlement ends appeal rights for both sides by consent. The TREC's claim that the tribes were barred from appealing while the government could appeal is contradicted as a description of the statute; whether a specific request to reserve appeal rights was refused in this settlement was not checked. The settlement cite is 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162, not 612.

instrument: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861, 12 Stat. 1163 (Art. 11 struck by Senate Aug. 6, 1861; assent dated [Oct. 29, 1861], 12 Stat. 1168); Kappler II 807
quote: and Cheyennes by the citizens of Denver City and the adjacent towns,
summary: Article 11, struck Aug. 6, 1861, asked that citizens of Denver City and adjacent towns be allowed to enter the town lands at $1.25 an acre; the assent is printed with an editor-supplied bracketed date [Oct. 29, 1861]. The erasures, date changes and misrepresented signatures are the Tribes' reading of the original, which the printed text cannot test. Unrau (1964:305) independently reads Article 11 as a device to get around the public-land laws.

citation: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, 1868; Fort Laramie treaty 1851 Art. 5; Peace Commission Report 1868, p. 6; Kappler II (1904) 594
quote: thousands of fortune-seekers, who possessed nothing more than the right of transit over these lands, took possession of them for the purpose of mining, and, against the protests of the Indians, founded cities
summary: The 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory ran to the main range of the Rockies, and the federal Peace Commission (1868) agreed the 1858-61 miners had only a right of transit and took the land over Indian protests. "Legally titled" and "never compensated" are tribal positions: the 1861 and 1865 treaties ceded the area on paper and the ICC paid compromise awards for it. The 100,000-trespasser, 4-million-acre school land and 19,000-acre CSU figures were not checked.

nations: Eastern Shoshone (Washakie's Band); Comanche; Ute; Navajo
citation: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, Fort Bridger, July 2, 1863, Art. 4; Kappler II 849 (18 Stat. 685), Art. 4
quote: the north Park or Buffalo House; and on the south,
summary: Primary text supports Shoshone-described limits reaching North Park and the Yampa River in 1863. The AD 1300 occupation date and pre-1800 extent rest on J. Donald Hughes via a Peter Faris article (secondary of secondary) and were not checked.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 97
quote: range from the waters of Wind river [sic] or latitude 43 30' on the north and from the South Pass to the headwaters of the North Platte on the east, and to Bear river [sic] near the mouth of Smith's Fork on the west.
summary: Explorer F.W. Lander's 1859 description of Eastern Shoshone range gives mappable limits: north to Wind River waters (lat 43 30), east from South Pass to North Platte headwaters, west to Bear River near Smith's Fork, south to Brown's Hole.

nations: Eastern Shoshone (Washakie's Band); Sioux; Cheyenne; Arapaho; Crow
instrument: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851, Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 as cited by Kappler
citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie with Sioux, etc., Sept. 17, 1851 (Kappler II); Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.), preamble
quote: the Sioux or Dahcotahs , Cheyennes , Arrapahoes , Crows , Assina- boines , Gros- Ventre Mandans , and Arrickaras , parties of the second part
summary: About 80 Shoshone men with families, led by Washakie and accompanied by Jim Bridger, came to the 1851 council though not invited. The Superintendent ruled them outside his instructions, so they were not parties to the treaty; they received presents and went home.

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie, 1851, Art. 2 (Kappler II); Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.), Art. 2
quote: The aforesaid nations do hereby recognize the right of the United States Government to establish roads, military and other posts, within their respective territories.
summary: Because the Shoshone were not party to the 1851 treaty, the report argues Article 2 (roads and military posts), Article 5 (boundaries) and free-passage provisions never applied to them, so trails and rights-of-way through Shoshone land had no treaty basis until 1863.

citation: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868; 15 Stat. 673, 674, Art. II
quote: rights in and to any portion of the territory of the United States, except such as is embraced within the limits
summary: The PSL author asserts land in present Colorado still belongs to the Shoshone. As a matter of treaty text, Art. II of the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty relinquished all title, claims or rights to any territory outside the Wind River reservation, which includes any Colorado lands described in 1863. The 1863 treaty did not cede land, and the Supreme Court held in 1945 that the 1863 Shoshone treaties did not recognize Indian title. Map this only as the author's claim, not as unceded land.

instrument: Stansbury, Exploration and Survey of the Valley of the Great Salt Lake (Senate print 1852); Reports of Explorations and Surveys (12 vols., 1854-61), Vol. II (Beckwith/Gunnison, 1855)
citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 99-101
quote: The path for the railroad was determined through Shoshone and other tribal lands without permission or a treaty, and over ten years before the Treaty of 1863.
summary: Federal survey expeditions mapped routes, including the future railroad route, through Shoshone and Ute lands without permission or treaty, over ten years before 1863. Congress printed 10,000 copies of the survey reports, which the report says spurred settler and miner rushes.

citation: Pacific Telegraph Act, June 16, 1860; 12 Stat. 41, ch. 137
quote: one quarter-section of land, such stations not to exceed one in fifteen miles
summary: The Pacific Telegraph Act was approved June 16, 1860 (not June 15). It let the contractor use 'unoccupied public lands of the United States' for right of way and repair stations of up to one quarter-section, about one per fifteen miles. It did not grant land outright. The line crossed Shoshone country in 1861 with no Shoshone treaty; the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty Art. 3 then agreed the existing telegraph might continue.

instrument: Act of July 5, 1862, 12 Stat. 512, 529; Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335 (1945)
citation: Shoshone Indians v. United States; 324 U.S. 335 (1945)
quote: only secure freedom from molestation for the routes of travel
summary: The Supreme Court (Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335, decided March 12, 1945, argued Nov. 10 and 13, 1944) recited that the 1862 commission was told the treaty was not expected to extinguish Indian title but only to secure safe travel routes and an acknowledgment of boundaries set as far from the routes as practicable. PSL's 'decided December 1945' is wrong.

instrument: 12 Stat. 489 (Pacific Railway Act); 12 Stat. 392 (Homestead Act); 12 Stat. 503 (Morrill Act)
citation: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862; 12 Stat. 489, sec. 1-2
quote: between the south margin of the valley of the Republican River and the north margin of the valley of the Platte River
summary: The 1862 Pacific Railway Act chartered a central route from the 100th meridian in Nebraska Territory west to Nevada, not a 32nd parallel route, and directed the United States to extinguish Indian titles to lands needed for the right of way and grants 'as rapidly as may be'. The link between these acts and the need for the 1863 treaty is the PSL author's argument.

citation: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes); PSL pp. 104-107
quote: Doty, Lincoln, Young and Connor were all instrumental and I feel conspired together to force the 1863 signing of the treaty at Fort Bridger with all of the Shoshone bands.
summary: Shoshone historian Darren Parry (Northwestern Band) says he feels Doty, Lincoln, Brigham Young and Connor conspired to force the 1863 treaties. This is his interpretation, quoted in the PSL report; it is not established by documents checked here.

citation: ARCIA 1863 (Commissioner Dole); Treaty with Northwestern Bands of Shoshoni, Box Elder, July 30, 1863; ARCIA 1863 p. 37-38; Kappler II 850-851
quote: Much credit is due to General Connor and the forces under his command, for their prompt and efficient services in chastising these Indians
summary: Bear River (Jan. 29, 1863) was carried out by Col. Connor's California Volunteers; the Commissioner credited Connor with forcing the bands to sue for peace. A treaty did follow: at Box Elder, July 30, 1863, the northwestern bands assented to the Fort Bridger treaty; it ceded no land. That Brigham Young took control of the land through the massacre is PSL's interpretation.

instrument: Union Pacific grading contract, Brigham Young (School of Prophets) and Samuel Reed
citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 107
quote: On May 21, 1868 (nearly two months before the Eastern Shoshone signed the 1868 Treaty) a contract was signed by Brigham Young
summary: About two months before the 1868 treaty, Brigham Young contracted with Union Pacific for about $2,125,000 to build railroad grade from near the Wyoming border to the Great Salt Lake, with his sons and attorney as subcontractors.

instrument: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863, 18 Stat. 685; Kappler II 848 (1904 ed.)
citation: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II); Kappler II 848 (1904 ed.), Art. 4; 18 Stat. 685
quote: on the east, by the Wind River mountains, Peenahpah river, the north fork of Platte or Koo-chin-agah, and the north Park or Buffalo House;
summary: Art. 4 recognizes Shoshone country as described by the nation: north, mountains north of the Snake River valley; east, Wind River Mountains, Peenahpah River, North Fork of the Platte (Koo-chin-agah), and North Park (Buffalo House); south, Yampa River and Uinta Mountains; west undefined, but present bands claimed to Salt Lake. This includes Colorado land.

citation: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II); Kappler II 848-849 (1904 ed.), Arts. 2-3
quote: it is stipulated by said nation that said railway, or its branches, may be located, constructed, and operated, without molestation from them, through any portion of the country claimed by them.
summary: Articles 2-3 opened routes, military posts, settlements, ferries, and retroactively accepted telegraph and stage lines already built, plus a future railway, through 'any portion of the country claimed by them'. The report reads this as a cover for prior unconsented use.

citation: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II); Kappler II 849 (1904 ed.), Arts. 5-6
quote: annually for the term of twenty years, the sum of ten thousand dollars, in such articles as the Presi¬ dent of the United States may deem suitable
summary: Art. 5 promised $10,000 a year for 20 years in articles the President chose, accepted 'as a full compensation and equivalent for the loss of game, and the rights and privileges hereby conceded'. Art. 6 acknowledged $6,000 in provisions and clothing already received as presents. Claims about failed appropriations and delays are the author's and were not checked against appropriation acts.

citation: Shoshone Indians v. United States; Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, July 2, 1863 (Kappler II); 324 U.S. 335 (1945); Kappler II 849 (1904 ed.), Art. 7
quote: an additional article was added to each and, except for one treaty not further involved here, accepted by the Indians.
summary: The treaty text as reproduced includes Article 7, limiting Shoshone title to what existed under Mexican law, under the heading 'Amendment ending Mexican agreements'. This appears to be a Senate-added article.

quote: Some identified more land in Colorado than that identified by Doty's map.
summary: Three maps of 1863 Shoshone country disagree: Doty's map presented to the Senate (made 1859, likely from War Department mapping of 1850), O. Stewart's 1957 map, and Dr. Joseph Robertson's 2023 Royce 520 overlay. Later maps show more Colorado land than Doty's.

citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5 (Kappler II); Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868; Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.), Art. 5; 15 Stat. 673, Art. II
quote: thence along the main range of the Black Hills and Wind River Mountains to the head- waters of the Yellowstone River
summary: The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty described Crow territory as running along the Wind River Mountains (it recognized, rather than granted, Crow country). The 1863 Fort Bridger treaty recorded Shoshone-described country but granted nothing; it was the 1868 Fort Bridger treaty that set apart the Wind River reservation for the Shoshone, with a separate future reservation for the Bannock. The Washakie and Big Robber duel at Crowheart Butte is tradition.

instrument: Instructions of Commissioner William P. Dole to Supt. O.H. Irish, March 1865
citation: Commissioner Wm. P. Dole to Supt. O.H. Irish, March 28, 1865, in Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1865; ARCIA 1865, Utah Superintendency, No. 29, pp. 148-149
quote: inasmuch as it has not been the policy of government to acknowledge the full title of these Indians to the lands claimed by them
summary: On March 28, 1865 Commissioner Dole told Superintendent Irish that, because the government's policy had not been to acknowledge the full title of the Utah Indians to the lands they claimed, treaties should have them relinquish the right of occupancy within defined boundaries and move to reserved lands. Dole did not say the government had never accepted Indian title to any land in Utah.

instrument: 15 Stat. 673 (concluded July 3, 1868; ratification advised Feb. 16, 1869; proclaimed Feb. 24, 1869); Kappler II 1020 (1904 ed.)
citation: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868; 15 Stat. 673, 674, Art. II
quote: commencing at the mouth of Owl creek and running due south to the crest of the divide between the Sweetwater and Papo Agie rivers
summary: Art. II set apart the Shoshone reservation 'for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the Shoshone, with a mappable boundary, and the Shoshone relinquished all other territory. Bannock reservation to be in Port Neuf and Kansas Prairie country.

citation: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes); PSL p. 124
quote: the over 40 million acres of ground taken from the Eastern Shoshone was not adequately compensated for in the 1868 Treaty.
summary: The PSL author argues the Eastern Shoshone relinquishment in 1868 was not adequately compensated. The acreage (over 40 million) and dollar valuations are the author's rough estimates and should not be mapped as figures. The 1868 treaty Art. II relinquishment is general and does not mention Colorado.

citation: United States v. Shoshone Tribe, 304 U.S. 111 (1938); 304 U.S. 111 (No. 668, decided Apr. 25, 1938); 85 Ct. Cls. 331
quote: No. 668. Argued March 31, April 1, 1938.-Decided April 25, 1938.
summary: The cited "Court of Claims No. H-129 (decided Dec 2, 1938)" does not match: the Supreme Court decided the Shoshone valuation case on Apr. 25, 1938 (No. 668) on review of 85 Ct. Cls. 331. Undelivered goods, school funds and the 1910 bribery claim are the author's impressions, unsourced.

citation: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868; 15 Stat. 673, 676, Art. XI
quote: unless executed and signed by at least a majority of all the adult male Indians occupying or inter- ested in the same
summary: Article XI requires any future cession of the reservation to be signed by a majority of adult male Indians occupying or interested in it. The author notes neither 1863 nor 1868 treaty itself had that requirement, and the Northern Arapaho were later included in the 1870s.

instrument: 18 Stat. 291 (Act of Dec. 15, 1874, ch. 2); ICC Docket No. 63
citation: Act of Dec. 15, 1874 confirming Brunot agreement of Sept. 26, 1872 (Kappler I); Shoshone Tribe v. United States; 18 Stat. 291; Kappler I 153-155 (1904 ed.); 299 U.S. 476, 487
quote: previous to and since the date of said treaty, mines have been discovered, and citizens of the United States have made improvements within the limits of said reservation
summary: The 1872 Brunot agreement, confirmed Dec. 15, 1874, ceded the southern part of the 1868 reservation (700,642 acres per the Supreme Court, about 23 percent of the 3,047,730-acre 1868 reservation, so about a quarter, not 'nearly a third') after miners and settlers had already moved in, as the agreement's own preamble admits. Payment was $25,000 in stock cattle over five years plus a $500 yearly salary to Washakie for five years ($27,500). The ICC (Docket 63, Aug. 20, 1954, as quoted in PSL) valued the land at $0.80 an acre ($560,513.60) and found the consideration unconscionable.

instrument: 24 Stat. 388 (General Allotment Act); 33 Stat. 1016 (Act of March 3, 1905)
citation: United States v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians; 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
quote: there were allotted to members of the tribes 245,058 acres
summary: Allotment carved parts of the Wind River reservation into individual parcels; the Supreme Court records 245,058 acres allotted to tribal members from 1907 to 1919. The opening of 'surplus' land to non-Native homesteaders came through the 1904 agreement ratified by the Act of March 3, 1905 (33 Stat. 1016), under which the US acted as trustee to sell the land, not through the Dawes Act itself or a sale to the government.

citation: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12 (Agreement with Shoshone and Arapahoe, April 21, 1896); 30 Stat. 62, 93-96

summary: Shoshone and Arapaho ceded a 10-by-10-mile tract including the Big Horn Hot Springs and its water rights. Congress accepted it only as amended, binding when the tribes agreed to the amendment.

citation: Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States; 299 U.S. 476, 487-488 (1937)

summary: The Indian Bureau settled the Northern Arapaho permanently at the Shoshone Agency in 1878. Shoshone attorney George Tunison argued this was done without Shoshone approval, and that from then on the government treated both tribes as equal beneficiaries, sharing Shoshone cession payments and allotments.

citation: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, 299 U.S. 476 (1937); Agreement of Apr. 21, 1896; 299 U.S. 476, 477 (syllabus); 30 Stat. 62, 93-94, ch. 3, sec. 12
quote: he treated the two tribes as equal beneficiaries of the reservation
summary: The 1896 agreement was made jointly with the Shoshone and Arapahoe tribes and paid $60,000 to both, but the Supreme Court found the Commissioner had treated the tribes as equal beneficiaries since the Arapaho were settled there on Mar. 18, 1878, over Shoshone protest. Stamm's claim that 1896 first made them equal partners, and that the Arapaho came with Shoshone consent, is not supported.

citation: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12; 30 Stat. 94-95, Arts. II-III
quote: the sum of sixty thousand dollars, to be expended for the benefit of the said Indians in the manner hereinafter described.
summary: The tribes ceded about 100 square miles around the Big Horn Hot Springs for $60,000 ($10,000 per capita/cattle; $50,000 in five annual installments for 'civilization' and rations at the Secretary's discretion). Signed by Washakie, Sharp Nose and 271 others (273). Tribes conceded partly because the Big Horn Basin buffalo grounds had been destroyed by cattle and sheep ranches from 1879.

citation: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12; 30 Stat. 95

summary: The interpreter certified that some signature names were duplicates but represented different individuals, and the acting agent (an Army captain) certified the 273 signers were a majority of adult males of both tribes combined. Majority was counted across both tribes, not per tribe. The source reproduces this without comment.

citation: Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, sec. 12; 30 Stat. 93, 96

summary: Congress ratified the 1896 agreement as amended, granting one mile square around the main hot spring to the State of Wyoming and declaring the rest public land open only under homestead and town-site laws. The chunk gives no evidence the tribes consented to the amendment.

citation: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452 (Agreement of April 21, 1904); 33 Stat. 1016, 1019
quote: is four hundred and eighty-four (484), of whom two hundred and eighty-two (282) have signed the foregoing agreement.
summary: McLaughlin sought cession of about 1.48 million acres north of the Wind River. After Arapaho leader Lone Bear left because his wife was ill, many Arapaho left with him; McLaughlin obtained signatures from 202 of 247 Shoshone men but only 80 of 237 Arapaho men, a majority of all men combined but a small minority of Arapaho.

quote: Articles II, III, and IX, which are amended and modified as follows
summary: After ratification, Lone Bear telegraphed Washington that the ratified version did not match what the tribe had signed. Separately, Mondell's legislation never promised to pay the tribes for the land; the US only acted as broker selling to settlers.

instrument: 33 Stat. 1016, sec. 2; Presidential proclamation of 1906 (not checked)
citation: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452, sec. 2; 33 Stat. 1016, 1021
quote: June fifteenth, nineteen hundred and six
summary: The 1905 Act set the opening of the ceded lands for June 15, 1906 by presidential proclamation. Revenue figures ($2.2 million projected, about $500,000 received), the elders' 1906 protest and the 1909/1914 sale percentages are from the WyoHistory.org article quoted in PSL and were not checked against primary records.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 141
quote: Construction was financed by money that Mondell managed to have allocated to it that year from Congress' annual appropriations meant for Indian reservations.
summary: The Indian irrigation system promised from 1905 land sales was never completed. In 1919 the Reclamation Service took over and built the Riverton Project (now Midvale Irrigation District) for settlers, financed with money Mondell had allocated from Congress' appropriations meant for Indian reservations.

citation: Wyoming v. EPA, Nos. 14-9512, 14-9514 (10th Cir. 2017) (amended opinion Nov. 7, 2017); 875 F.3d 505 (10th Cir. 2017)
quote: approximately seventy-five percent of the land affected by the 1905 Act is held in trust by the United States
summary: The Tenth Circuit held Congress intended the 1905 Act to diminish the reservation, excluding Riverton and land north of the Wind River; the Supreme Court denied cert in 2018. Interior's Solicitor and EPA had concluded the 1905 Act did not change the 1868 boundaries. Judge Lucero dissented that the lands were held in trust and about 75% of the opened lands remain in trust.

citation: Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States; 299 U.S. 476 (1937), No. 216, decided Jan. 4, 1937
quote: gress the jurisdictional Act of March 3, 1927, under which they
summary: Congress allowed the Shoshone to sue by the jurisdictional Act of March 3, 1927 (ch. 302), not 1928. On Jan. 4, 1937 the Supreme Court held that putting the Arapaho on the Shoshone reservation was a taking of a Shoshone property interest requiring just compensation, with interest. The settlement terms requiring Shoshone recognition of Arapaho residence, and the renaming to 'Wind River', are book only.

instrument: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, 85 Ct. Cls. 331; affirmed, 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
citation: United States v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians; 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
quote: Minerals and standing timber are constituent elements of the land
summary: The Court of Claims valued the Shoshone one-half interest (1,171,770 of 2,343,540 acres) taken for the Arapaho on March 19, 1878 at $1,581,889.50, including timber and minerals. The Supreme Court (Butler, J.) affirmed in 1938 that the 1868 treaty gave the tribe the mineral and timber rights.

quote: Not to exceed $1,000,000 of said judgment fund
summary: The Act of July 27, 1939 credited $2,450 to each enrolled Shoshone member: $100 available at once, $1,350 per adult (or $500 per minor) for land, homes, livestock and similar purposes, and the remainder under Interior rules (minors' shares held until age 18). Up to $1,000,000 of the judgment fund could buy land. The 'about $4.2 million' net figure is book only.

citation: Act of Dec. 15, 1874, ch. 2 (Kappler I); 18 Stat. 291; Kappler I 153 (1904 ed.)
quote: An Act to confirm an agreement made with the Shoshone Indians (eastern band ) for the purchase of the south part of their reservation
summary: This chunk contains no body text on the Lander/Brunot cession; it appears only in endnotes 89-90 (body text is in the prior chunk) and in the Fed. Cir. 2004 description of the reservation as 1868 lands 'minus certain lands sold to the United States in 1872 and 1896.'

instrument: ICC Docket 63, 3 Ind. Cl. Comm. 313 (findings), 333 (opinion), Aug. 20, 1954
