summary: The ICC docket for the Wind River Shoshone is cited (endnote 91) but discussed in the prior chunk, not here. No award amount appears in this chunk.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 138
quote: Only about 10 percent of the Reservation is owned by non-Indians.
summary: The tribes sued the US for breach of trust in mismanaging mineral resources and trust funds. The court described the reservation as retaining Indian character with only about 10% owned by non-Indians. Outcome of the claims is not stated in the source.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 136
quote: rejected it by a vote of 339 for and 469 against on June 15, 1935
summary: The Wind River Shoshone and Arapaho rejected the IRA 339 for, 469 against, on June 15, 1935. Sovereignty resides today in each tribe's General Council. The author argues non-IRA tribes were less controlled by the BIA.

instrument: 753 P.2d 76 (Wyo. 1988), aff'd by an equally divided Court, 492 U.S. 406 (1989); 835 P.2d 273 (Wyo. 1992)
citation: Wyoming v. United States; 492 U.S. 406 (1989)
quote: 753 P. 2d 76, affirmed by an equally divided Court.
summary: Big Horn I (753 P.2d 76, Wyo. 1988) recognized the tribes' 1868 reserved (Winters) water right; the US Supreme Court affirmed by an equally divided Court in Wyoming v. United States, 492 U.S. 406 (1989) (decided June 26, 1989). The Big Horn III ruling against instream use is 835 P.2d 273 (Wyo. 1992). PSL's '49 U.S. 406' is a typo.

citation: Herrera v. Wyoming; 587 U.S. ___, No. 17-532 (May 20, 2019), syllabus
quote: The Crow Tribe’s hunting rights under the 1868 Treaty did not expire upon Wyoming’s statehood.
summary: The Supreme Court held the Crow Tribe's 1868 treaty hunting right did not expire at Wyoming statehood and vacated and remanded. PSL's phrase 'treaty rights are not extinguished at statehood' paraphrases the holding. The 2023 dismissal and HB 83 history are book only.

nations: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation;Shoshone;Bannock
instrument: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation v. Wooten, No. 22-35140 (9th Cir. 2023)
citation: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation v. Wooten, No. 22-35140 (9th Cir. Oct. 17, 2023); No. 22-35140, slip op. 5
quote: plainly do not condition exercise of the reserved hunting right on the Northwestern Band relocating to a reservation.
summary: The Ninth Circuit held the 1868 treaty's hunting right is not conditioned on a band relocating to a reservation, and remanded. The opinion recites that the Shoshone used over 80 million acres in Idaho, Colorado, Utah, Nevada and Wyoming 'from time immemorial.'

quote: east of the Green River and north of Yampa the two maps diverge by 40 or 50 miles toward Steamboat Springs
summary: Dr. Joseph Robertson (Mato Ohitika Analytics, 2023) compared the 1859 Doty map of Shoshone territory, presented to the Senate for the 1863 treaty, with Royce's area 520 and found the two diverge by 40 to 50 miles east of the Green River and north of the Yampa, toward Steamboat Springs. The author suggests both maps may be inaccurate and this could support Shoshone claims.

citation: Executive Order 13007, Indian Sacred Sites, May 24, 1996; 61 Fed. Reg. 26771 (May 29, 1996)
quote: accommodate access to and ceremonial use of Indian sacred sites by Indian religious practitioners
summary: EO 13007 citation confirmed. The rock art, medicine wheel, Tarnesse identification and Washakie visits were not checked. Browns Park NWR is a USFWS refuge; Vermillion Canyon is largely BLM land, not "BLM as a National Wildlife Refuge".

citation: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes); PSL pp. 148, 161 (TREC Recommendation 2)
quote: I further recommend that the Vermillion Canyon and Brown’s Park sites be placed into East Shoshone Trust.
summary: The author recommends Eastern Shoshone co-management with Interior, FWS and BLM under EO 13007 and SO 3403, and that Vermillion Canyon and Browns Park be placed in Eastern Shoshone trust; Colorado is asked to cooperate.

citation: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act, June 30, 1834; 4 Stat. 729, ch. 161
quote: This economic loss has never been included in any compensation for the violation of Shoshone rights.
summary: TREC recommends compensating the Eastern Shoshone for trespass 1834-1868 under the 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act. The 1834 Act (4 Stat. 729, ch. 161) is the correct cite. Shoshone country in Colorado is northwestern, not northeastern, Colorado as the recommendation says. Whether 1834 'Indian country' covered Shoshone lands then claimed by Mexico (south of 42 N before 1848) or Oregon Country is a legal question the recommendation does not address.

instrument: Congressionally funded exploration (incl. Gunnison-Beckwith 1853), roads, telegraph, railroads
citation: PSL TREC 2024 report (Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes); PSL pp. 161, 163 (TREC Recommendation 3)
quote: any abandoned railroad and other such lands be returned to the Tribes that owned that land before Treaties took it from them
summary: TREC asks Colorado to acknowledge that Shoshone and other tribal land was mapped illegally 1824-1863 by congressionally ordered expeditions, enabling land theft and illegal roads, telegraph lines and railroads, and asks that abandoned railroad lands be returned to the tribes.

citation: Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock, July 3, 1868; 15 Stat. 673, 674-675, Arts. II and IV
quote: right to hunt on the unoccupied lands of the United States so long as
summary: TREC argues the treaties never specifically relinquished Shoshone hunting, fishing, water and mineral rights in Colorado. The 1868 treaty does reserve a right to hunt on 'the unoccupied lands of the United States' generally (Art. IV), but Art. II relinquishes 'all title, claims, or rights' to territory outside the reservation, so the claim that Colorado water and mineral rights were never released is an untested legal theory.

citation: Great Outdoors Colorado Board, December 2025 meeting minutes; GOCO Board resolutions, Dec. 2025
quote: Exercise its discretionary authority to award funding to the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe
summary: Tribes are not recognized as eligible entities under Colo. Const. art. XXVII, but the GOCO board has discretionary authority to fund them and used it in Dec. 2025. The recommendation stands as policy advice; the USFS 200-site figure is unsourced.

citation: Act of March 3, 1905, ch. 1452, Art. IX as amended; 33 Stat. 1016, 1020-1021
quote: it being the understanding that the United States shall act as trustee for said Indians to dispose of said lands
summary: Congress never promised to pay the tribes for the 1905 lands; the only promise was that Interior would broker sales to settlers. The promised irrigation system for tribal lands south of the river depended on these sales and was never completed.

citation: ARCIA 1896, Report of Shoshone Agency; ARCIA 1896, Shoshone agency report (Aug. 20, 1896)
quote: In April last Inspector McLaughlin concluded a treaty with the Shoshones and Arapahoes for the cession of the Big Horn Hot Springs
summary: Prime buffalo hunting grounds in the Big Horn Basin were destroyed by an influx of cattle and sheep ranches from 1879, so the tribes no longer hunted there; this loss was a reason they were willing to cede the hot springs in 1896.
reason_not_supported: The 1896 agent report records the cession but gives no reason tied to loss of Big Horn Basin hunting to ranches. Stamm's account; McLaughlin's council proceedings (Sen. Doc. 247, 54th Cong., 1st Sess.) would be the decisive source and were not found. Not mappable.

nations: Tabeguache Ute; Kapuuta (Capote) Ute; Moughwach (Mouache) Ute; Weeminuche Ute; Grand River Ute; Yampa Ute; Uintah Ute
instrument: 13 Stat. 673 (concluded Oct. 7, 1863; amendments assented Oct. 8, 1864; proclaimed Dec. 14, 1864)
citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863; 13 Stat. 673, 676, 678
quote: UN-COW-RA-GUT, or Red Color,
summary: Ten Ute men signed the Oct. 7, 1863 treaty as 'chiefs and warriors of the Tabeguache band' (13 Stat. 676), Ouray (U-ray) among them. On Oct. 8, 1864 nine Tabeguache men assented to the Senate amendments, six from the 1863 list plus three new names. Attendance by other bands (Kapuuta, Mouache, Weeminuche walkout, Kaniache's refusal) is from PSL, not the treaty. The treaty still ceded all Tabeguache-claimed lands outside the reserve, including areas other bands used.

citation: ARCIA 1863, Gov. Evans report (Colorado Superintendency); ARCIA 1863 p. 124, 130
quote: the chiefs of his band who visited Washington last spring, having secured the result
summary: A Tabeguache delegation did visit Washington in spring 1863 and no treaty was made there; the treaty followed at Conejos on Oct. 7, 1863. Evans described the delegates as chiefs and headmen of Head's band. That Head packed the delegation with men without standing, and that it refused to negotiate without consulting the bands, was not found in ARCIA 1863.

citation: ARCIA 1863, Colorado Superintendency reports; ARCIA 1863 p. 123-150
quote: recently returned from their visit to Washington, who told their brethren that
summary: A Ute delegate rejected terms in Washington, saying the US wanted Ute land for gold and offered only copper; the delegation went home without a treaty, insisting on consulting their people first.
reason_not_supported: The gold-for-copper speech does not appear in ARCIA 1863; the official account says returning delegates urged peace. Speaker and record unidentified. Do not map as a quote.

nations: Tabeguache Ute; Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute
citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863 (witness list); 13 Stat. 676
quote: J. W. Chroug hton , Col. 1st Cav. of Col’do, Comd’g Dist.
summary: Officers of the 1st Colorado Cavalry witnessed the 1863 treaty, including the colonel commanding the district (printed 'J. W. Chroughton, Col. 1st Cav. of Col'do, Comd'g Dist.') and Lt. Col. Samuel F. Tappan. Chivington held exactly that post in 1863, so the printed name is likely a misprint for Chivington, but this is not confirmed here. The figure of 500 soldiers is from PSL and was not checked.

nations: Tabeguache Ute; Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute
instrument: 13 Stat. 673 (Senate amendments of March 25, 1864; assent Oct. 8, 1864)
citation: Report of Gov. A. Cummings, Colorado Superintendency, in Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1866; Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863; ARCIA 1866 p. 155; 13 Stat. 673, 677-678
quote: They say that the boundaries of the lands surrendered by them, as well as of the lands reserved to them, are not in accordance with their understanding.
summary: The Senate's amendments of March 25, 1864 struck the part of the reserve boundary that ran through the San Luis Valley (Sandy Creek, the Rio Grande between 106 and 107 W), so the San Luis Valley lands left out of the reserve were ceded. Nine Tabeguache men signed an assent to the amendments on Oct. 8, 1864. In 1866 the Tabeguache told Gov. Cummings the treaty was not the one they agreed to and that the amendments were never shown to them in readable form; Cummings reported that the interpreters and Agent Head agreed with them. So 'altered without consent' is supported in substance (an assent that was not informed), but not as a treaty changed with no assent at all.

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863; 13 Stat. 673, 674, Art. II
quote: relinquish all of their claim, right, title, and interest in and to any and all of their lands within the territory of the United States, wherever situated, excepting that which is included within the following boundaries
summary: The 1863 treaty ceded all Tabeguache-claimed lands outside the reserve described in Art. II. Since the recital of Tabeguache country ran along the base of the Rockies from the 37th to the 41st parallel and included North and Middle Park, the cession took the Front Range and parks east of the Continental Divide and Middle Park, including Pikes Peak (Tava). The treaty does not name Tava or Pikes Peak; that identification and its sacred meaning come from PSL.

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863, Art. III and Senate amendments; 13 Stat. 673, 674, 677
quote: in any part of the country hereby retained by said Indians, where gold or other metals or minerals may be found
summary: The 1863 treaty itself let any US citizen mine without interference anywhere in the land reserved to the Tabeguache, and let the US place military posts and roads on unceded lands. The reservation was open to mineral entry from the start.

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863, Art. IV; 13 Stat. 673, 674, Art. IV
quote: the Mohuache band of Utah Indians may also be settled with them upon the lands and hunting-grounds reserved in this treaty
summary: Art. IV records the Tabeguache consent that the Mouache 'may also be settled with them' on the reserve. It does not require the Mouache to move. The link to Kaniache's refusal to negotiate is PSL's inference ('probably').

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863, Senate amendments and assent; 13 Stat. 673, 676-678
quote: as against all other Indian tribes
summary: Per the Jorjani memo (M-37051), the Senate amended the 1863 treaty so Ute exclusive rights in the reserved lands held only against other tribes, and so the US admitted no greater Ute title than existed at the Mexican cession. The chunk does not say whether the Tabeguache assented to these amendments.

instrument: 9 Stat. 922, 930; 9 Stat. 984; Hayt v. United States, 38 Ct. Cl. 455 (1903)
citation: Solicitor's Opinion M-37051, Feb. 21, 2018; M-37051, n. 9 (citing Hayt v. United States, 38 Ct. Cl. 455, 460-465 (1903))
quote: Mexican law did not consider "aboriginal title" of any particular Indian group beyond a right of occupancy within their accustomed territories.
summary: Jorjani memo states Mexican law recognized no aboriginal title for groups like the Ute beyond occupancy, and the US did not treat the area as Indian country until treaties and reservations created it. This is the federal legal premise that made Ute land 'public' at cession.

citation: Treaty with the Utah, Dec. 30, 1849 (Abiquiu); 9 Stat. 984, Arts. I, V-VII
quote: designate, settle, and adjust their territorial boundaries
summary: The 1849 Abiquiu treaty (Senate consent and proclamation Sept. 9, 1850) had the Utes acknowledge US jurisdiction and 'unconditionally submit', gave free passage, and let the US set up military posts and agencies. It did not set boundaries: Art. VII says the US would later 'designate, settle, and adjust their territorial boundaries' and the Utes would then confine themselves within them. It ceded no land.

citation: Treaty with the Utah, Dec. 30, 1849; 9 Stat. 984, 985
quote: QUIXIACHIGIATE, his x mark,
summary: The printed 1849 treaty lists Quixiachigiate first of 28 named 'principal and subordinate chiefs, representing the Utah tribe' (he plus 27 others, not 28 subordinates). The printed spelling with an 'x' is confirmed; whether he was the Capote chief or Kaniache (Omer Stewart's misprint theory, per PSL) is not settled by the treaty text.

citation: Treaty with the Utah, Dec. 30, 1849 (witnesses); 9 Stat. 984, 985
quote: J. H. Whittlesey, 1st Lieut. 1st. Dragoons.
summary: Lt. J.H. Whittlesey of the 1st Dragoons signed as a witness to the Abiquiu treaty, confirmed. The jailing of Kaniache and the dragoon attack north of Taos are from PSL and were not checked.

citation: Treaty with the Utah, Dec. 30, 1849, Art. VIII; 9 Stat. 984, 985, Art. VIII
quote: adopt such other liberal and humane measures, as said government may deem meet and proper
summary: The Abiquiu treaty did not promise fixed annuities. Art. VIII said the US would give 'donations, presents, and implements' and other measures 'as said government may deem meet and proper', in return for Ute performance. PSL's point that expected goods did not arrive and hunger followed is book only.

citation: Greiner to Calhoun, Taos, Oct. 20, 1851 (postscript); Abel, Official Correspondence of James S. Calhoun (1915) p. 438
quote: preparations are being made by the Citizens of this Valley & others, to settle the lands claimed by the Eutaws in the Valley of the Los Conejos.
summary: Greiner wrote that citizens were preparing to settle lands "claimed by the Eutaws" in the Conejos valley, and that the Utes had repeatedly driven Mexicans off and would not give it up quietly. The Utes forced to retreat (to Ojo Caliente) after Kiowa and Arapaho raids were a band near Red River, not the Conejos lands. PSL's quote is altered.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 402
quote: It is unclear whether Carson purposefully infected the Ute leaders, but given his later activities against the Navajo and other Indigenous Peoples, it is not outside the realm of possibility.
summary: After an 1854 council where Ute leaders received presents including blanket coats, all the chiefs present, including Chico Velasquez, died of smallpox and an epidemic followed. PSL says it is unclear whether Carson deliberately infected them, but calls it not impossible.

nations: Moughwach Ute; Kapuuta Ute; Jicarilla Apache
quote: Government attorneys ultimately dismissed all claims for restitution based on the fact that claimants were unlawfully in Indian country.
summary: PSL reframes the 1854 Christmas Eve attack on El Pueblo by Tierra Blanca as retaliation for starvation and broken Abiquiu promises, and notes the US dismissed settler depredation claims because claimants were unlawfully in Indian country.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 404
quote: capturing over 50 women and children, who were probably placed in Anglo and Mexican households as slaves.
summary: Col. Thomas Fauntleroy surprised a camp near Poncha Pass on April 28, 1855, killing forty warriors. The campaign then destroyed lodges and captured over 50 women and children, probably placed as slaves in Anglo and Mexican households. Some sources report mutilation and Ute women killing their children to avoid capture.

instrument: Unratified Treaty with the Mohuache Utahs, Sept. 11, 1855 (NARA T494)
citation: Treaty with the Mohuache Band of Utahs, Sept. 11, 1855, and Meriwether to Manypenny, Sept. 15, 1855 (unratified); Unratified treaty, Sept. 11, 1855, Art. III (Avalon Project)
quote: These Indians did not appear to be in so destitute a condition as the Jicarillas
summary: The Mouache treaty was signed Sept. 11, 1855 (not August) and ceded all Mouache claims in New Mexico except a reservation (Art. III); it was never ratified. Meriwether reported the Mouaches less destitute than the Jicarillas, though they had lost many people and horses. The mule-eating detail and the settler petition to Pierce were not found.

nations: Moughwach Ute; Tabeguache Ute; Kapuuta Ute
citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 405
quote: This was the last and only hunting region left to the Moughwach, Tabeguache, and Kapuuta bands.
summary: The Pikes Peak gold rush pushed the Tabeguache out and by 1859 miners were in South Park, the last hunting area of three bands, years before the 1863 cession. Supt. J.L. Collins said citizens, not the army, should handle the 'Indian problem'.

nations: Grand River Ute; Yampa Ute; Uintah Ute
citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863 (recital of Tabeguache country); 13 Stat. 673, preamble
quote: running thence northerly with the base of the Rocky Mountains to the forty-first parallel of north latitude
summary: PSL says the Grand River, Yampa and Uinta Utes were not yet under any treaty in 1862 and sent no delegates in 1863. The 1863 treaty nonetheless recited Tabeguache country as reaching the 41st parallel and taking in North and Middle Park, and ceded all of it outside the reserve. As amended by the Senate, the claim was exclusive only 'as against all other Indian tribes'. That the parks were Grand River and Yampa country is PSL's band description; the treaty claims them as Tabeguache.

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863, Art. II and Senate amendments; 13 Stat. 673, 674, 677
quote: the source of the Sandy Creek of the San Louis valley; thence down the Sandy Creek to the place where its waters sink at low water
summary: The Art. II reserve as signed in 1863 ran from the Uncompahgre mouth down the Gunnison, up the 'Bunkara' and Roaring Fork, along the Arkansas-Gunnison divide, then via Sandy Creek of the San Luis Valley to the Rio Grande at 106 W, up the Rio Grande to 107 W and south to the San Juan divide. The Senate struck the Sandy Creek and Rio Grande segment (the quoted words) and changed 'Arkansas' to 'Gunnison's Fork of the Great Colorado', so the reserve as ratified excluded the San Luis Valley. Map the ratified reserve, not the signed one.

citation: Treaty with the Tabeguache Band of Utah Indians, Oct. 7, 1863, preamble; 13 Stat. 673
quote: Beginning on the 37th degree of north latitude, at the eastern base of the Sierra Madre Mountains ; running thence northerly with the base of the Rocky Mountains to the forty-first parallel of north latitude
summary: The treaty recited Tabeguache country as running from the 37th parallel at the base of the Sierra Madre north along the Rockies to the 41st parallel, west to the Snowy Range, south via Rabbit Ears to the Grand River, down to the Gunnison and Uncompahgre, then south to the La Plata range and back along the 37th parallel.

nations: Grand River Ute; Uintah Ute; Yampa Ute; Muache Ute; Tabaguache Ute; Capote Ute; Weeminuche Ute
instrument: 15 Stat. 619 (concluded March 2, 1868; amendment July 25, 1868; assents Aug.-Sept. 1868; proclaimed Nov. 6, 1868)
citation: Treaty with the Ute, March 2, 1868, Senate amendment and assent; 15 Stat. 619, 623-626
quote: those of the Grand River and Uintah Ute Indians on the fifteenth day of August
summary: The 1868 Ute treaty was signed in Washington on March 2, 1868 by ten Ute men and amended by the Senate (July 25, 1868). Assent was collected by band: Grand River and Uintah Aug. 15, Yampa Sept. 1, Tabeguache and Mouache Sept. 14, Capote Sept. 24, Weeminuche Sept. 25. In the Statutes at Large the Tabeguache label sits beside the group led by Ou-ray and the Mouache label beside the group led by Ka-ni-ache, so PSL's reversal is a transcription error. The claim that no Capote signed the original is doubtful: Capote assent signer Ba-bu-zat appears to be original signer Pa-bu-sat.

Adams says he went to Greeley after consulting Ouray, with the Secretary's approval; meetings with Pitkin driving it were not found.

Article 17 of the 1868 treaty preserves benefits for any Ute who stays at peace. That the removal of the peaceful Uncompahgre "contradicts" Art. 17 is PSL's legal argument; formally the 1880 cession was an agreement ratified by Ute signatures, not a forfeiture under Art. 17.

But in the same passage he proposed using that title to buy them out: a commission to obtain their consent "to remove from the State to some other location, say to the Indian Territory", with payment from sale of their Colorado lands.

summary: The 1880 agreement sent the Uncompahgre to Grand River near the Gunnison "if a sufficient quantity of agricultural land shall be found there", and otherwise to land "in that vicinity and in the Territory of Utah". The commissioners assigned to the Uncompahgre selection (the report names Mears and Russell building the new agency and McMorris paying improvement claims) reported the Grand River land unsuitable. That this report was knowingly false and motivated by Mears's interest is PSL's accusation, not established by the primary record.

quote: shall be subject to entry under the desert, homestead, and town-site laws
summary: The Hunter Act opened the Southern Ute strip to homesteading and sale. Mouache and Capote took allotments; the Weeminuche under Ignacio refused allotment and moved west to Towaoc. Many allotments were later sold. Final Southern Ute boundaries set 1899.

citation: Act of Aug. 15, 1894, s.20 (28 Stat. 337); Act of June 7, 1897; 1898 appropriation act (Kappler I); 28 Stat. 337, s.20; 30 Stat. 62 (1897)
quote: the said Indians shall pay one dollar and twenty-five cents per acre for said lands from the fund now in the United States Treasury realized from the sale of their lands in Colorado
summary: The 1894 Act required the Uncompahgre to pay $1.25 per acre for allotments from their Colorado land fund. The Act of June 7, 1897 opened unallotted Uncompahgre lands to entry. A later act authorized approval of 83 allotments made after April 1, 1898. The Belt opinion is from H.R. Rep. 2967 (1890), not checked.

instrument: Act of May 1902; Act of March 1903 (allotment without consent); McLaughlin agreement 1903
citation: Kappler I (1902 Indian appropriation act, Uintah provisions); Act of May 27, 1902, ch. 888 (Kappler I 753)
quote: whenever a majority of the adult male Indians of said tribes shall have consented to the allotment of lands and the restora¬ tion of the unallotted lands within said reservation
summary: The 1902 Act required consent of a majority (not three-fourths) of adult males of the Uintah and White River Utes. McLaughlin's 82 of 282 signatures (Conetah via PSL) would fall short of that majority. The 1903 no-consent provision and the bribery and child-signer rumors are not checked.

citation: ARCIA 1907, "The Absentee Utes"; ARCIA 1908; ARCIA 1907 p. 125-130; ARCIA 1908 p. 119-121
quote: a band of about 200 nonprogressive Utes
summary: In 1906 a band of about 200 (the Wyoming governor said 300) mostly White River Utes left Uintah for Pine Ridge after allotment and the opening of their surplus lands. At Wyoming's governor's request troops took them to Fort Meade, then the Cheyenne River Reservation; 360 returned to Utah with Capt. Johnson in 1908. "About 400" and an alliance aim are not in ARCIA.

instrument: ICC Docket 349, 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707, 728 (1965); 21 Stat. 199
citation: ICC Docket 349, Findings of Fact on the Stipulated Settlement (Feb. 18, 1965); ICC Docket 349, 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707, Findings 1, 4
quote: had no obligation to furnish such a reservation
summary: In Docket 349 the Uncompahgre claim was that the US never gave them a reservation in Colorado or Utah as the 1880 agreement required; the US denied any such obligation. The case ended in a compromise settlement, a net $300,000 judgment after offsets, entered Feb. 18, 1965. It is a settlement, not a finding that the US failed its obligation.

nations: Confederated Bands of Ute Indians (excluding Uintah)
instrument: ICC Docket 327, 11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 180, 222 (1962); final judgment 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 706 (1965)
citation: ICC Docket 327, Findings of Fact Part 2 (Sept. 14, 1962); ICC Docket 327, 11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 180, 222, Findings 35, 51-53
quote: The Commission finds that, as of April 29, 1874, Royce Area 566 had a fair market value in the amount of $8,500,000.00.
summary: For Royce 566 the ICC rejected Ute experts' valuation of $40,773,533, set value at $8,500,000 and offset $507,662.84 previously paid, despite vast later mineral extraction.

citation: Act of May 14, 1884, ch. 50; 23 Stat. 22
quote: section eight of an act entitled “An act to accept and ratify the agreement submitted by the confederated bands of Ute Indians in Colorado
summary: The 1884 Act repealed section 8 of the 1880 Act and restored the lands referred to in it to the public domain. The ICC Docket 327 exclusion language ("not included in the cession") could not be checked. The 10,240 acres (16 sq. mi.) matches the 1876 executive order tract.

instrument: ICC Docket 328; Court of Claims Case 46640 (1950 consent judgment); US v. Southern Ute Tribe, 423 F.2d 346 (Ct. Cl. 1970); US v. Southern Ute Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971)
citation: United States v. Southern Ute Tribe or Band of Indians, 402 U.S. 159 (1971); 402 U.S. 159, 160, 164, 174
quote: We therefore hold that the claim in this case is res judicata under the 1950 consent judgment enforcing the settlement agreement
summary: The ICC rejected the Government's res judicata defense in 1966 (17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 28) and again on remand in 1969 (21 Ind. Cl. Comm. 268); the Court of Claims affirmed (423 F.2d 346). The Supreme Court reversed (Douglas dissenting), holding that the plain wording of the 1880 Act ceded all nonallotted land including the Southern Ute strip (Royce 617), so the 1950 consent judgment (Case No. 46640, 117 Ct. Cl. 433) barred the claim. The attorney in the 1950 stipulation is called "Dr. Wilkinson"; Ernest L. Wilkinson and Glen A. Wilkinson represented the Utes in this era. Charles Wilkinson is wrong.

citation: ICC Docket 328, Findings of Fact (May 6, 1966); ICC Docket 328, 17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 28, Finding 14; final order 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 10 (1971)
quote: No interest was paid on any part of the money deposited in the fund
summary: Trust fund 'Indian Moneys, Proceeds of Labor, Southern Ute Indians' ($19,124.22) earned no interest until 1931 per the tribe; misuse claims the ICC said required accounting disappeared with the 1971 dismissal.

citation: Luebben, in The Indian Claims Commission (as quoted by PSL); PSL p.455 n.21 (Luebben 2006)
quote: hundreds of millions of acres outside of recognized reservation boundaries remained subject to tribal title in 1946
summary: Quoting attorney Thomas Luebben: the ICC could never return land, may have foreclosed quiet title actions, and served termination and assimilation; hundreds of millions of acres remained subject to tribal title in 1946.

nations: Ute Tribes (Southern Ute, Ute Mountain Ute, Uncompahgre/Northern Ute)
citation: PSL TREC 2024, Ute recommendations; PSL pp.463-466
quote: support the Ute Nations in their quest to have the Indian Claims Commission’s decisions governed by the Congress opened for appeal
summary: Eleven TREC recommendations: state compensation for trespass and illegal pre-cession mining; federal restoration of treaty water rights (Winters); state compensation to Uncompahgre for forced removal; unrestricted hunting, fishing and plant gathering on all public lands; compensation or restoration of railroad easements; restitution for descendants of enslaved Utes (Lafayette Head); GOCO funding access; no state property tax on enrolled Utes; support reopening ICC decisions to appeal (Dockets 44, 45, 327, 328); tuition, room and board waivers.

citation: PSL TREC 2024, p. 465
quote: children were stolen by Lafayette Head, the Indian Agent for Colorado, who participated in the slave trading of children
summary: TREC states Indian Agent Lafayette Head participated in slave trading of Ute children; recommends compensation for descendants.

citation: Treaty with the Six Nations, 1784 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 15, Art. I; Kappler II 5
quote: Six hostages shall be immediately delivered to the commissioners by
summary: Article I of the 1784 Fort Stanwix treaty made peace conditional on the Senecas, Mohawks, Onondagas and Cayugas delivering six hostages, to be held until all prisoners were returned; the Art. III boundary followed in the same instrument. The treaty text does not itself show the hostages were already in custody at signing, and the later Six Nations repudiation of the delegates comes from secondary accounts (atlas V003), not from this text.

citation: Treaty with the Wyandot, etc., 1785 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 16, Art. I and VI; Kappler II 6
quote: Three chiefs, one from among the Wiandot, and two from among the
summary: Article I required three chiefs (one Wyandot, two Delaware) to be held by the US commissioners until all prisoners were restored. Article VI had the signers acknowledge that lands east, south and west of a reserved Wyandot-Delaware tract (between the Cuyahoga and the Great Miami) belonged to the US. That is the southern, eastern and far western parts of present Ohio, not "most of Ohio". The "never carried into effect" catalog note was not verified.

citation: Treaty with the Shawnee, 1786 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 26, Art. I; Kappler II 16
quote: Three hostages shall be immediately delivered to the Commissioners, to remain in the possession of the United States until all the prisoners
summary: Article I required three Shawnee hostages until all prisoners were returned (confirmed in the treaty text). The black wampum incident (Clark knocking it down and grinding it underfoot) and the threat of war come from accounts based on Richard Butler's treaty journal and were not checked against that journal here; present them as Butler's account.

citation: Treaty with the Shawnee, Jan. 31, 1786 (Fort Finney); 7 Stat. 26, Arts. I-II
quote: Three hostages shall be immediately delivered to the Commissioners
summary: The treaty text confirms terms dictated to the Shawnee: Article I required three hostages to be delivered at once until captives were returned, and Article II made the Shawnee acknowledge US sovereignty. Partial attendance, reluctant signing by Moluntha's people and later renunciation remain secondary.

nations: Wyandot; Delaware; Ottawa; Chippewa; Potawatomi; Sauk
citation: Treaty with the Wyandot, etc., 1789 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 28, Art. I-II; Kappler II 18
quote: two persons of the Wyandot Nation, to be retained in the hands of the United States as hostages, until the said prisoners are restored
summary: Article I required the nations to deliver two Wyandot persons as hostages to Governor St. Clair, held until prisoners were restored. The treaty re-confirmed the Fort McIntosh line, and the Shawnee and Miami, who were fighting the US, were not party.

nations: Wyandot; Delaware; Shawnee; Ottawa; Chippewa; Potawatomi; Miami; Eel River; Wea; Kickapoo; Piankeshaw; Kaskaskia
citation: Treaty of Greenville, 1795 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 49, Art. II; Kappler II 39
quote: ten chiefs of the said tribes shall remain at Greeneville as hos
summary: Article II required ten chiefs to remain at Greenville as hostages until American prisoners were delivered. The treaty, ceding most of Ohio, followed Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers (Aug. 1794) and the burning of towns and crops along the Maumee and Auglaize.

citation: G. A. Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), ch. 13; 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II 977
quote: I determined to seize the most prominent chiefs as hostages for the fulfilment of their promises regarding the corning on of the villages
summary: Custer's own memoir says he seized Lone Wolf and Satanta, who had met his column under a flag of truce, as hostages to force their villages to come in to Fort Cobb, and told them they would die if their tribe did not come in. The quoted line "I then arrested both him and Lone Wolf and held them as hostages" was not found in the Kansas Collection text of chapters 13-15; use the wording above. The release date (about Feb. 1869) was not checked.

citation: NPS, Washita Battlefield NHS, History & Culture; 15 Stat. 593; Kappler II 984
quote: quickly retreated to Camp Supply with his captives - 53 women and children
summary: Custer's troops took 53 Cheyenne women and children captive at the Washita (NPS). NPS says the loss of winter supplies "forced many bands to accept reservation life". The claim that the captives were used as hostages or human shields to drive bands onto the reservation is historians' interpretation not found in the NPS page; attribute it to the named historian before mapping as HOSTAGE.

citation: George A. Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), Project Gutenberg 73498; Custer, My Life on the Plains (1874), ch. on Sweetwater (March 1869) and Fort Hays
quote: if by sunset the following day the two white girls were not restored to our hands unharmed, the lives of the three chiefs would be forfeited
summary: On the Sweetwater in March 1869 Custer seized four Cheyenne men as hostages, released one as a messenger, and told the rest their lives would be forfeited unless the two white captives were returned by sunset the next day. The three chiefs (Custer names Big Head, Dull Knife and Fat Bear) were taken to Fort Hays. There, during a transfer to the guard-house, a fight broke out with the guard: Big Head was killed, Dull Knife died of a bayonet wound, and Fat Bear survived and was later released.

quote: He killed eighty-six men women, and children and took seventy hostages
summary: Gen. William Harney attacked Little Thunder's Brule camp, killing about 86 men, women and children and taking about 70 hostages (mostly women and children). Harney then dictated terms to Lakota bands at Fort Pierre in 1856 while captives were held.

citation: Treaty with the Navajo, 1868 (Statutes at Large); 15 Stat. 667; Kappler II 1015
quote: The actual cost of the removal of the tribe from the Bosque Re- dondo reservation to the reservation
summary: The 1868 treaty was signed at Fort Sumner while the Dine were held at Bosque Redondo, and it paid for their removal home to a reservation while they relinquished the right to occupy territory outside it (Royce 519 ceded, 518 reserved). The Barboncito quotation and Sherman's Indian Territory proposal come from the council proceedings, not the treaty, and were not checked. The death toll ("up to about 3,500") and population (8,000-10,000) were not verified.

citation: NPS Nez Perce NHP, Aftermath of the Flight of 1877; 14 Stat. 647 (the 1863 treaty enforced)
quote: Although they expected to be able to return home upon surrender, those 432 nimíipuu were sent to Fort Leavenworth in Kansas that winter
summary: After Bear Paw, 432 Nimiipuu who surrendered (not about 400), expecting to go home, were sent to Fort Leavenworth and then Indian Territory; after about eight years they returned in 1885, some to Lapwai and others, including Joseph, to Colville. The Joseph quotation about Miles's promise was not re-read here.

nations: Muscogee (Creek) Nation (allied 'friendly' Creeks and absent Red Sticks)
citation: Treaty of Fort Jackson, 1814 (Kappler II); NPS article by Kathryn Braund; 7 Stat. 120; Kappler II 107
quote: Whereas an unprovoked, inhuman, and sanguinary war, waged by the hostile Creeks against the United States
summary: Styled a capitulation, the treaty was made with the Creek National Council, a US ally; the Red Sticks who fought were largely dead or in Florida. Jackson took about 21-23 million acres from both factions as payment for the war.

nations: Nimiipuu (Nez Perce): Lawyer's treaty faction; Wallowa (Old Joseph), White Bird, Looking Glass, Toohoolhoolzote bands
citation: Royce 1899 entry for the 1863 Nez Perce treaty (atlas crosswalk); 14 Stat. 647; Kappler II 843
quote: The Nez Perce tribe relinquish to the U. S. the lands heretofore reserved for their use and occupancy, excepting so much thereof as is hereinafter set apart for a new reservation.
summary: The 1863 treaty relinquished the 1855 Nez Perce reservation except a much smaller new reserve (Royce 441 ceded, 442 retained). That it was signed by Lawyer's faction after the non-treaty bands left, and ceded the Wallowa and other homelands of bands that never signed, is the standard account (NPS/Greene) but the NPS page could not be retrieved here. The quoted line in the row is a paraphrase, not a source quote; the 90 percent and 700,000-acre figures were not checked.

citation: MNHS, 'The Traders' Paper' (U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 site); MNHS Traders' Paper page; 10 Stat. 949
quote: turned over about a third of the Dakotas' cash payments to a group of traders, including Henry Sibley and his associates
summary: After signing the Traverse des Sioux treaty in 1851, Sisseton and Wahpeton leaders signed a separate Traders' Paper that some later said they were tricked into signing; it assigned about a third of their cash payments to traders including Henry Sibley's associates. The claim that the 1852 annuity was withheld until the Dakota accepted the settlement is not on the MNHS page and was not checked in a primary source.

citation: Treaty of Medicine Creek, 1854 (Statutes at Large), signature block; 10 Stat. 1132; Kappler II 661
quote: LESH-HIGH, his x mark.
summary: Leschi and Quiemuth reportedly refused to sign, yet X marks appear by their names; some hold that Stevens's party forged them, others that Leschi signed under protest. Leschi objected that the Nisqually reservation was rocky high ground cut off from the river.

nations: Nisqually; Puyallup; Duwamish; Suquamish; Snohomish; others (Stevens treaties)
citation: Treaty of Medicine Creek, Dec. 26, 1854; Treaty of Point Elliott, Jan. 22, 1855; 10 Stat. 1132; 12 Stat. 927
quote: explained using the Chinook trading jargon, which only had a vocabulary of about 300 to 400 words
summary: Treaty texts confirm the instruments but say nothing about the language of interpretation. The Chinook Jargon interpretation is the standard account of the councils; the 300 to 400 word figure is a critic's estimate reported by Crosscut, not a primary fact.

nations: Yakama (14 bands); Cayuse; Umatilla; Walla Walla; Nez Perce
citation: Yakama Treaty, 1855 (Statutes at Large); NPS article Walla Walla Council 1855; 12 Stat. 951; 12 Stat. 945; 12 Stat. 957
quote: with Kamaiakun as its head chief, on behalf of and acting for said tribes and bands
summary: Stevens and Palmer cajoled and threatened delegates; interpreter Andrew Pambrun said Stevens told Kamiakin that refusal meant walking 'in blood knee deep', and that Kamiakin signed in such a rage he bit his lips bloody. The Yakama treaty made Kamiakin a head chief over 14 bands he did not lead.

citation: Treaty with the Winnebago, 1837 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 544; Kappler II 498
quote: The said Indians agree to remove within eight months from the ratification of this treaty
summary: The treaty text says the Ho-Chunk would remove "within eight months from the ratification" (confirmed). That the delegation lacked authority, was kept in Washington and refused passage home, believed it had eight years, and that the interpreter admitted deception come from secondary accounts and were not checked against a primary record.

citation: Treaty with the Osage, Nov. 10, 1808 (Fort Clark); 7 Stat. 107; Kappler II 95
quote: White Hair was a "government chief" who had no authority to make binding agreements for the tribe
summary: Treaty text confirms the Nov. 10, 1808 cession at Fort Clark. The claims that Osage leaders rejected Clark's September version because they were absent and that White Hair was a 'government chief' without authority rest on secondary sources.

citation: Report of the Ute Commission, in Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs 1881; ARCIA 1881, Report of Ute Commission pp. 203-204; 21 Stat. 199
quote: the names obtained at both agencies aggregated 581 adult male Ute Indians of the confederated bands in Colorado
summary: The Ute Commission's own report confirms the Southern Utes at first refused to ratify, Ouray died on Aug. 24, 1880 during the councils, and the commission then gathered marks band by band until it counted 581 adult males, which it judged above three-fourths. Mears was a member and disbursing officer. The report says nothing about $2-per-signature payments; that claim rests on Conetah as quoted by the PSL book.

instrument: Agreement of Oct. 6, 1892, ratified as amended by Act of June 6, 1900, 31 Stat. 672, 676
citation: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903), statement of the case; 187 U.S. 553
quote: On October 6, 1892, 456 male adult members of the confederated tribes signed
summary: 456 adult men signed the 1892 Jerome agreement and the agent certified 562 adult men. The higher count of 639 comes from a January-February 1893 payment roll (725 males over 18, 639 aged 21 and over) cited by the Secretary of the Interior, not from a 1900 census. The opinion records the tribes' claim that their assent was obtained by "fraudulent misrepresentations of its terms by the interpreters"; counterfeit or altered signatures are not in the opinion.

citation: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903), syllabus; 31 Stat. 672; 187 U.S. 553
quote: cannot be adjudged to materially limit and qualify the controlling authority of Congress
summary: Congress changed the 1892 agreement before enacting it, without returning it to the tribes, and the Court held Congress could do so regardless of Article 12.

citation: Act of March 3, 1893, ch. 203, ratifying the Kickapoo agreement of June 21, 1891; 27 Stat. 557, ch. 203, pp. 557-563
quote: when I explained it to said Whipple he pretended to interpret it to said Indians, in full council assembled
summary: The ratified text confirms the Kickapoo insisted on going to Washington to put their demand for a diminished reservation held in common to the Secretary of the Interior. The interpreter, Joseph Whipple, signed his certificate by mark; his certificate says he speaks and understands English and Kickapoo. Attorney John T. Hill certified that Whipple 'pretended to interpret' the power of attorney. The text does not say the interpreter certified that he could not read or write.

nations: Lakota; Dakota; Nakota (Great Sioux Reservation bands); Santee
citation: Minot State University digital 'A History of the Sioux Agreement
quote: did not tell the Indians that, by signing the paper they were giving up land
summary: The Edmunds commission (with interpreter Samuel Hinman) sought about half the Great Sioux Reservation; a contemporary history says signers were not told they were giving up land. The agreement failed to gain the 3/4 signatures and was never ratified.

citation: Treaty of Payne's Landing, 1832 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 368; Kappler II 344
quote: should they he satisfied with the character of that country, and of the favor
summary: The treaty made removal conditional on a Seminole delegation finding western land suitable and on Seminole merger with the Creeks. Five of the most important chiefs, including Micanopy, did not agree to removal.

citation: Treaty with the Seminole, Fort Gibson 1833 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 423; Kappler II 394
quote: hereby declare themselves well satisfied with the loca
summary: At Fort Gibson the seven-man exploring delegation declared itself "well satisfied" with the western location and agreed the nation would begin removal. That they were authorized only to inspect and report, were coerced, and that most Seminole repudiated it comes from Florida Memory and a quoted 1830s letter, not from a primary read here.

citation: Treaty with the Creeks, 1826, preamble (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 237; Kappler II 214 (annulled by 7 Stat. 286, Kappler II 264)
quote: have represented that the same was signed on their part by persons having no sufficient authority to form treaties, or to make cessions
summary: Signed by a minority under William McIntosh, in violation of a Creek National Council law (which McIntosh had voted for) making unauthorized cession a capital offense. The Senate ratified it anyway on Mar. 7, 1825; Gen. Gaines later agreed the signers had no authority, and McIntosh was executed under Creek law.

citation: Treaty with the Creeks, 1826, Art. 1-2 (Kappler II); 7 Stat. 286; Kappler II 264
quote: is hereby declared to be null and void, to every intent and purpose whatsoever
summary: The 1826 Treaty of Washington annulled Indian Springs, the only ratified Indian treaty so annulled, but in Art. 2 still ceded most Creek land in Georgia east of the Chattahoochee. It did not take all of it: a remaining strip was ceded by the treaty of Nov. 15, 1827 (Royce 141). Georgia's survey threat is secondary context.

nations: Seneca (Seneca Nation; Tonawanda Band); Tuscarora; other Haudenosaunee in NY
citation: The Case of the Seneca Indians in the State of New York (Philadelphia, 1840), Joint Committee of Friends; 7 Stat. 550; Kappler II 502
quote: Large bribes were offered to such of the chiefs as could be deceived by misrepresentation, or gained by the love of money
summary: The Quaker Joint Committee concluded Seneca signers were bribed by Ogden Land Company agents; a New York Senate resolution calls the treaty fraudulent through bribery, forgery and deception. The Senate ratified it anyway; the Friends published 'The Case of the Seneca Indians' (1840).

nations: Seneca Nation; Tonawanda Band of Seneca
citation: Treaty with the Seneca, 1842 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 586; Kappler II 537
quote: the Cattaraugus Reservation containing by estimation twenty-one thousand six hundred and eighty acres of land
summary: The 1842 compromise returned Allegany and Cattaraugus to the Seneca while confirming the loss of Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda. Tonawanda later bought back part of its land under the treaty of Nov. 5, 1857 (11 Stat. 735; Royce 40). That Tonawanda "never consented" is the Tonawanda position and is not stated in the 1842 text.

citation: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, 1830, supplementary articles (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 333; supplementary articles 7 Stat. 340; Kappler II 310
quote: SUPPLEMENTARY ARTICLES TO THE PRECEDING TREATY.
summary: The Sept. 28, 1830 supplementary articles grant sections of land to named persons presented by the chiefs. That this was done after most of the assembled Choctaw had left and served as inducements to signers is historians' interpretation; the text does not say so and no named scholar was read here.

nations: Cherokee Nation (Treaty Party vs. National Council)
citation: Gilcrease Museum, John Ross Papers catalog; DocsTeach (NARA); 7 Stat. 478; Kappler II 439
summary: New Echota was signed by a Treaty Party minority without National Council authority while Principal Chief John Ross was away. The 15,665-signature memorial was presented to Congress in 1838, after the Senate ratified the treaty in May 1836; the National Archives DocsTeach petition cited in the row is a different, earlier petition with 3,352 signatures. The one-vote ratification margin was not checked against the Senate Executive Journal.

citation: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (BAE 19th Annual Report, 1900); 7 Stat. 93; 7 Stat. 95; Kappler II 82-84
quote: recorded as a part of the treaty, but not embodied in the copy sent to the Senate for con- firmation
summary: Commissioners won over chiefs Doublehead and Tollunteeskee with secret articles reserving valuable tracts for them, which were not included in the copy sent to the Senate. Doublehead was later killed by Major Ridge and others under a decree of the Cherokee chiefs for abusing his office.

citation: Treaty with the Chippewa, Sept. 24, 1819 (Saginaw); 7 Stat. 203; Kappler II 185
quote: Cass supplied 5 barrels of whiskey
summary: Treaty text confirms reserves to named individuals. That they were trader Jacob Smith's children, that Cass supplied five barrels of whiskey, and that Cass led the Saginaw to believe they kept their lands come from a modern court filing (U.S. v. Michigan) and later claims, not from the treaty.

nations: United Nation of Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi
citation: Royce 1899 Schedule, Sept. 26, 1833, Chicago; Treaty of Chicago; Royce 1899, Chicago Sept. 26, 1833 entry; 7 Stat. 431; Kappler II 402
quote: supposed to contain about 5,000,000 acres
summary: Royce confirms the united Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi ceded their land along the western shore of Lake Michigan (about 5,000,000 acres) for a tract of not less than 5,000,000 acres west of the Mississippi. The schedules in the treaty pay large sums for claims. The 1902 Wisconsin Potawatomi petition and the liquor and trader-capture details were not checked.

citation: Black Hawk, Life of Ma-ka-tai-me-she-kia-kiak (1833; Quaife ed. 1916); Treaty of St. Louis 1804 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 84; Kappler II 74
quote: They had been drunk the greater part of the time they were in St. Louis.
summary: A small delegation sent to St. Louis to secure release of a Sauk man held for murder signed a cession of a huge area between the Mississippi and Illinois rivers. Sauk and Meskwaki custom required an elaborate council process; Black Hawk always denied the delegates' authority, and some signers later said they had been intoxicated.

citation: Black Hawk, Life of Ma-ka-tai-me-she-kia-kiak (1833; Quaife ed. 1916); 7 Stat. 141; Kappler II 126
quote: I touched the goose quill to the treaty — not knowing, however, that, by that act, I consented to give away my village
summary: Black Hawk signed the 1816 peace treaty, which reconfirmed the 1804 cession; he later said he did not know that by signing he was giving away his village of Saukenuk.

citation: Treaty with the Sauk and Foxes, 1832 (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 374; Kappler II 349
quote: partly as indemnity for the expense incurred, and partly to secure the
summary: Signed Sept. 21, 1832, seven weeks after Bad Axe, the treaty demanded the cession "partly as indemnity" for the war. Article VII held Black Hawk, his two sons, the Prophet and others as named hostages "for the future good conduct of the late hostile bands", so this row should also be tagged HOSTAGE. The 400-square-mile reserve in Art. II was for the confederated tribes and was drawn to include Keokuk's principal village; it was not a personal grant to Keokuk.

instrument: 7 Stat. 323; Kappler II 300 (and 7 Stat. 315 for the 1828 provisional agreement)
citation: Treaty with the Winnebago and United Tribes of Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa, Aug. 25, 1828 (Green Bay); 7 Stat. 315, preamble; Kappler II 292
quote: the occupation, by white persons, of that part of the mining country which has not been heretofore ceded to the United States
summary: The 1828 Green Bay agreement records that the Winnebago and the United Tribes declined to cede, and that a provisional boundary was set to deal with white occupation of unceded mining country. The 1829 Prairie du Chien treaty (7 Stat. 323) then ceded the lead region. Red Bird's imprisonment and the 1827 war are not in these texts.

instrument: Kappler IV 1065 (full text with signatures); Kappler II 594
citation: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851, full text with signatures; 11 Stat. 749 (text as printed in Kappler IV 1065-1067), Art. 6
quote: having selected principals or head chiefs for their respective nations, through whom all national business will hereafter be conducted
summary: Article 6 records that each nation had 'selected' a head chief through whom all national business would be conducted, and binds the nations to sustain those chiefs. The first Sioux signer is Mah-toe-wha-you-whey (Conquering Bear). That the commissioners picked him and Big Robber when the nations would not, and that most Lakota did not recognize his authority, rests on secondary sources.

instrument: Colonial (Crown) deed, Nov. 5, 1768; quoted in Royce 1899 p. 584
citation: Royce 1899, introduction (C. Thomas), New York, quoting the Fort Stanwix deed of 1768; Royce 1899 p. 584, quoting the deed of Nov. 5, 1768 (N.Y. Colonial Documents vol. 8)
quote: beginning at the Mouth of Cherokee or Hogohege River where it emptys into the River Ohio and running from thence upwards along the South side of said River to Kittaning
summary: The 1768 Fort Stanwix deed, quoted in Royce's introduction, records the Six Nations granting to the Crown the land south and east of a line beginning at the mouth of the Cherokee (Tennessee) River and running up the Ohio to Kittanning.
