summary: AP confirms: $1.7 trillion of homelands, more than $546 million in state mineral revenue, 10 tribal nations with 'aboriginal title, congressional title, and treaty title to lands within Colorado', the quoted finding, and recommendations including resolving illegal transfers, compensation, restored hunting and fishing rights, and a 0.1% real estate fee. The claim that the Arapaho and Cheyenne 'never gave up mineral rights' is not in the AP story and was not found; drop it unless the PSL book supports it.

citation: MNHS, 'Traders' Paper' (U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 site); 10 Stat. 949; 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819; MNHS Traders' Paper page; 10 Stat. 949; Act of Feb. 16, 1863, ch. 37, 12 Stat. 652; Act of Mar. 3, 1863, ch. 119, 12 Stat. 819
quote: they were ushered to another document, which some later said they were tricked into signing. The Traders’ Paper, as the document is known, turned over about a third of the Dakotas’ cash payments to a group of traders, including Henry Sibley
summary: Confirmed: Traders' Paper (about a third of cash payments, Sibley among traders), 1863 abrogation and forfeiture (12 Stat. 652: treaties 'abrogated and annulled' and lands and annuities 'forfeited') and removal act (12 Stat. 819). Fixes: the 2021 return was about 114 acres (reports range 114 to 120), not 'about 120'. MNHS also notes the Senate struck the 1851 reservation provision before ratification, so the Minnesota River reservation rested on later presidential and congressional action, not the 1851 treaty text as signed.

citation: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946, 60 Stat. 1049, secs. 2, 15, 22; 60 Stat. 1049, sec. 2, sec. 15, sec. 22
quote: The payment of any claim, after its determination in accordance with this Act, shall be a full discharge of the United States of all claims and demands touching any of the matters involved in the controversy.
summary: ICC awards were money only; return of land was excluded. Value was fixed at the date of taking (often 19th-century prices) and generally without interest; awards were reduced by 'gratuitous offsets' for past federal spending; attorney fees came out of awards; tribes bore the burden of proof and research costs. Accepting an award, or a dismissal, extinguished the claim.

citation: Johnson v. M'Intosh, 21 U.S. 543 (1823); City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005); Joint Note of the Dicasteries for Culture and Education and for Promoting Integral Human Development on the 'Doctrine of Discovery' (Mar. 30, 2023); 21 U.S. (8 Wheat.) 543, 587; 544 U.S. 197, 203 n.1; Holy See Press Office Bulletin 230330b
quote: The “doctrine of discovery” is not part of the teaching of the Catholic Church.
summary: Johnson quote is accurate but Marshall phrases it as the US position the Court accepts: 'They maintain, as all others have maintained, that discovery gave an exclusive right to extinguish the Indian title of occupancy, either by purchase or by conquest' (21 U.S. at 587). Sherrill does not cite Johnson by name; its footnote 1 invokes the 'doctrine of discovery' through Oneida II (470 U.S. 226, 234) and Oneida I (414 U.S. 661, 667). The Vatican note says the doctrine is not Church teaching, that the bulls 'have never been considered expressions of the Catholic faith', and that the Church 'repudiates those concepts that fail to recognize the inherent human rights of indigenous peoples, including what has become known as the legal and political doctrine of discovery'; it does not rescind the bulls. Correct 'cited in Sherrill' to 'the doctrine was invoked in Sherrill (2005)'.

citation: Synthesis of the batch sources; grep of atlas repo; (synthesis)
summary: This is the atlas team's synthesis, not a finding stated by the named works. The authors (Deloria, Williams, Echo-Hawk, O'Brien) critique federal legal vocabulary and its effects; they do not address this atlas, so 'the works agree the atlas should...' should read 'drawing on these works, the atlas will...'. Current repo counts: 98 'cessions', 58 'cession', 52 'ceded' (whole-word, case-insensitive).

citation: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, Calls to Action (2015); Senate Committee on Indian Affairs (Dec. 20, 2024); S. 761 (119th Cong.); TRC Canada, Calls to Action 45-49 (2015)
quote: We call upon federal, provincial, territorial, and municipal governments to repudiate concepts used to justify European sovereignty over Indigenous peoples and lands, such as the Doctrine of Discovery and terra nullius
summary: 94 Calls to Action confirmed. Discovery and terra nullius repudiation appears in Calls 45 (Royal Proclamation), 46 (Covenant of Reconciliation) and 47 (all governments), and in the church-related Calls 48-49. The 'cultural genocide' characterization of the Final Report was not re-checked here. US: the Truth and Healing Commission on Indian Boarding School Policies Act (S. 1723) passed the Senate on Dec. 20, 2024 but was not enacted; it was reintroduced as S. 761 (119th Cong., Feb. 26, 2025) and reported from committee; no enactment found.

nations: Pequot (Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation; Eastern Pequot Tribal Nation)
instrument: Colonial; Hartford covenant of 1638 (not in Kappler or Royce)
citation: John Mason, A Brief History of the Pequot War (Boston, 1736), archive.org briefhistoryofpe00maso; Mason 1736, pp. 30-31 and 38-39 (as reprinted)
quote: themselves utterly Destroyed, to the Number of six or seven Hundred, as some of themselves confessed. There were only seven taken captive, and about seven escaped
summary: Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay forces under John Mason and John Underhill, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, burned the fortified Pequot village at Mystic and killed those who fled. The 1638 Hartford treaty divided Pequot survivors and land among the victors and barred use of the Pequot name.

instrument: Conestoga Manor (Penn proprietary grant to Conestoga); no cession instrument located
citation: Benjamin Franklin, A Narrative of the Late Massacres in Lancaster County (1764)
quote: hearing that the remaining fourteen Indians were in the Work-houfc at Lancajler
summary: Paxton Boys (about 50 mounted settlers) killed 6 Conestoga at Conestoga Town, then on Dec 27 broke into the Lancaster workhouse and killed the 14 survivors held there for protection: 20 dead, the last of the community. No one was prosecuted.

nations: Lenape (Delaware) and Mohican Moravian Christian converts; descendants incl. Delaware Nation (OK), Delaware Tribe of Indians, Munsee-Delaware
instrument: Context only; Moravian tracts: ordinance of Sept. 3, 1788 and Act of June 1, 1796 (Royce 1899)
citation: John Heckewelder, A Narrative of the Mission of the United Brethren (1820); Royce 1899 Ohio remarks; Heckewelder 1820, preface; Royce 1899 (ordinance of Sept. 3, 1788; Act of June 1, 1796)
quote: after upwards of ninety of their number had been murdered by Williamson's party
summary: Heckewelder, a Moravian missionary, says upwards of ninety Christian Indians were murdered by Williamson's party, half of them women and children. Royce records that a Congressional ordinance of Sept. 3, 1788 set apart 4,000-acre tracts at Schoenbrunn, Gnadenhutten and Salem for the Society of United Brethren, patented to the society under the Act of June 1, 1796. The land link to McIntosh/Greenville is time sequence only.

citation: Encyclopedia of Alabama, Battle of Tallushatchee; 7 Stat. 120; Kappler II 107
quote: In all, 186 Red Sticks were killed, including a number of women and children.
summary: Gen. John Coffee's Tennessee militia (under Andrew Jackson) surrounded Tallushatchee and killed the town's men and some women and children; it opened the campaign that ended at Horseshoe Bend and the Fort Jackson cession.

nations: Muscogee (Creek), Red Stick towns (Upper Creek); Muscogee (Creek) Nation, Poarch Band descendants
citation: NPS Horseshoe Bend NMP, History & Culture; 7 Stat. 120; Kappler II 107
quote: By dark at least 800 of Chief Menawa's 1,000 Red Sticks were dead (557 slain on the field and 200-300 in the river).
summary: Jackson's army with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies destroyed the fortified Red Stick town of Tohopeka. Five months later Jackson dictated the Fort Jackson cession of about 20 to 23 million acres, signed largely by Creek leaders who had been US allies.

nations: Sauk; Meskwaki (Fox); Black Hawk's British Band; Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) context
citation: Treaty with the Sauk and Foxes, 1832, preamble (Statutes at Large); 7 Stat. 374; Kappler II 349
quote: partly as indemnity for the expense incurred, and partly to secure the
summary: At Bad Axe (Aug. 1-2, 1832) US troops, militia and the steamboat Warrior attacked Black Hawk's band, mostly families, at the Mississippi crossing; at least 150 died, with estimates up to about 300, and others drowned or were killed by Dakota across the river. Seven weeks later the 1832 treaty took the Iowa strip (Royce 175) expressly "partly as indemnity" for the war and held Black Hawk and others as hostages. The 400-square-mile reserve (Royce 226) was kept in 1832 and ceded in 1836.

instrument: None ratified. California 1851-52 treaties unratified (Senate rejected 1852)
citation: Wikipedia 'Sacramento River massacre
summary: John C. Fremont's US Army topographical expedition, with Kit Carson and local settlers, attacked a large gathering of Wintu on the Sacramento River, pinning women and children against the river. It came weeks before the US conquest of Mexican California.

instrument: 16 Stat. 707 (context only; verified as the 1864 Klamath-Modoc treaty)
citation: Oregon History Project (Oregon Historical Society), Fremont and Kit Carson at Upper Klamath Lake; 16 Stat. 707 (context only)
quote: Frémont and Kit Carson attacked and burned a Klamath village, killing 14 men.
summary: In May 1846, after an attack on Fremont's camp, Fremont and Carson attacked and burned a Klamath village at the Williamson River mouth, killing 14 men by Fremont's count (Oregon Historical Society); others say more, including women and children. Date is May 10 in Fremont's memoir account, May 12 in others. The 1864 Klamath treaty is later context, not a consequence.

date: 1849-03 (Battle Creek); 1850-02-08/1850-02-09 (Fort Utah) and following Spanish Fork executions
nations: Timpanogos (Utah Valley Ute); Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray descendants
citation: Act of May 5, 1864 (Statutes at Large); Royce 449-452; 13 Stat. 63
quote: An Act to vacate and sell the present Indian Reservations in Utah
summary: In February 1850 the Nauvoo Legion besieged a Timpanogos camp on the Provo River and then killed men who had surrendered or fled (Rock Canyon, Spanish Fork); estimates run from about 40 to over 100 dead. Utah Valley was later settled without a ratified cession; the small reserves of 1856-59 were vacated by the act of May 5, 1864 (13 Stat. 63) and restored to the public domain in 1878.

nations: Pomo (Clear Lake / Eastern Pomo, Habematolel); Robinson Rancheria, Habematolel Pomo of Upper Lake descendants
instrument: Unratified treaty, Camp Lu-pi-yu-ma, Aug. 20, 1851 (Kappler IV)
citation: Kappler IV, Unratified treaties: Treaty at Camp Lu-pi-yu-ma, Aug. 20, 1851, and Senate rejection resolution; Kappler IV 1084-1085 (schedule item O; Senate resolution of July 8, 1852)
quote: Treaty at Camp Lu-pi-yu-ma, August 20, 1851, made and concluded between Redick McKee, and the chief, captains and headmen of the Ca-la-na-po
summary: The unratified treaty for the Clear Lake bands was made by Redick McKee at Camp Lu-pi-yu-ma on the south side of Clear Lake, Aug. 20, 1851, and the Senate refused consent on July 8, 1852. The May 1850 Bloody Island attack and its toll (Lyon's report of about 60 versus later estimates up to 800) were not checked against Lyon's report.

date: 1853 (late fall per NAHC; one historian argues summer solstice)
instrument: None ratified; Tolowa included in no ratified treaty
citation: Federal Register NAGPRA notice, Mar. 11, 2014 (79 FR, doc. 2014-05322)
quote: One of the first and most brutal attacks occurred at Yan’daa-k’vt, while the people gathered for the Earth Renewal Ceremony, Nee-dash.
summary: A federal notice (2014), drawing on Tolowa Dee-ni' information, records a massacre at Yan'daa-k'vt (Burnt Ranch) during the Nee-dash ceremony, one of the first attacks of a Tolowa holocaust that began in 1851. Death estimates range widely (NAHC 20-600; often 450-600 in tribal accounts). The row's detail of a summer-solstice dating is one historian's view.

nations: Takelma; Rogue River bands (Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians; Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde descendants)
citation: Oregon Encyclopedia (Hungry Hill; Rogue River War) via search; SOHS; 10 Stat. 1018; Kappler II 603
summary: On Oct. 8, 1855, volunteers under James Lupton attacked a Takelma camp near Butte Creek before dawn; estimates run from 23-24 to 40 killed, about half women and children. It set off the 1855-56 Rogue River War and the 1856 removal north. Royce 407 is wrong for this link: 407 is the Grand Ronde reserve set up by executive order of June 30, 1857, not a cession; the Table Rock cession under 10 Stat. 1018 is Royce 312.

evidence_display: Reported by Wikipedia 'Mendocino War' and 'Walter S. Jarboe
nations: Yuki (Ukomno'm); Round Valley Indian Tribes descendants; also Wailaki, Nomlaki, Pomo in region
instrument: Nome Cult Farm / Round Valley Reservation (executive and statutory reservations, 1856 onward)
citation: Wikipedia 'Mendocino War' and 'Walter S. Jarboe
summary: With Gov. John Weller's permission, Walter Jarboe's Eel River Rangers raided Yuki communities for six months; Jarboe himself reported 283 'warriors' killed, not counting women and children, and the state paid the company. The Yuki were reduced to a few hundred and confined to Round Valley.

instrument: None. Land return: City of Eureka transfer 2019-10-21 (council vote Dec 2018)
citation: Wikipedia; Indianz; Cultural Survival
summary: Settlers attacked Tuluwat on Indian Island during the World Renewal Ceremony and other Wiyot villages the same night (Feb. 26, 1860), killing mostly women, children and elders. Estimates for the night range from about 60 to 250. No Wiyot land was ceded by a ratified treaty; Eureka returned the island to the Wiyot Tribe in 2019.

instrument: California militia appropriation and war-bond acts 1851-52 and later; federal reimbursement acts (Congress); Act for the Government and Protection of Indians 1850; 18 unratified 1851-52 treaties
citation: Newsweek 2016
summary: California financed about 24 militia campaigns against Native people between 1850 and 1861, spending roughly $1.29 to $1.5 million, and Congress reimbursed all but about $200,000. By Jan 1854 the state had already spent $924,259 on such expeditions; a later act appropriated up to $400,000 for nine campaigns of 1854-59 that killed at least 766 people.

nations: Dakota (Mdewakanton, Wahpekute, Sisseton, Wahpeton); Ho-Chunk (Winnebago) also removed
instrument: 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819; Act Feb 21 1863 (Winnebago) cite not checked
citation: Act of Feb. 16, 1863 (Statutes at Large); MNHS Historic Fort Snelling; 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819
quote: are hereby declared to be abrogated and annulled, so far as said treaties or any of them purport to impose any future obligation on the United States
summary: After the 1862 war (begun amid withheld annuities), about 1,600 Dakota noncombatants were held in a stockade below Fort Snelling where 130 to 300 died; Congress then voided the Dakota treaties, forfeited annuities and land, and ordered removal from Minnesota. The Minnesota River reserve (Royce 440) was taken and sold.

citation: MNHS, U.S.-Dakota War: The Trials & Hanging; 12 Stat. 652; 12 Stat. 819
quote: On December 26, 1862, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato.
summary: Thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged together after military commission trials, some lasting minutes; it is the largest mass execution in US history and was followed within weeks by treaty abrogation and removal.

nations: Ihanktonwanna (Yanktonai) Dakota; Hunkpapa Lakota; Sisseton, Wahpeton refugees; Standing Rock descendants
instrument: Context: Sully punitive expedition; later Fort Sully treaties 1865
citation: State Historical Society of North Dakota, Whitestone Hill State Historic Site
quote: Many Indian men, women, and children died or were captured.
summary: Gen. Alfred Sully's troops attacked a large camp gathered to hunt and dry meat, most of whose people had no role in the 1862 Minnesota war, killing 150 to 300 or more and destroying winter food stores.

nations: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation
citation: Royce 1899 entry 444 (Ruby Valley treaty, Western Shoshone); 13 Stat. 663; 18 Stat. 685; 18 Stat. 689
quote: No formal purchase of the territorial claim of these tribes or bands was made, but the U. S. took possession of the same
summary: Connor's California Volunteers attacked the Northwestern Shoshone winter camp at Boa Ogoi on Jan. 29, 1863, killing about 250 to 500 (estimates: about 250, about 350 per Utah Division of Indian Affairs, 400+ on markers). The 1863 Shoshone and Goshute treaties followed within nine months. The Royce quote and areas 444 and 447 concern the Western Shoshone (Ruby Valley) and Goshute, not the Northwestern Band, whose Box Elder treaty (13 Stat. 663) has no Royce area. The massacre-to-treaty link is a time sequence; no source here says the massacre caused those treaties.

date: 1862-03 (Alabama Hills raid); 1863 (killings under Capt. McLaughlin); 1863-07-10 forced march
nations: Owens Valley Paiute (Nuumu); Big Pine, Bishop, Lone Pine, Fort Independence Paiute descendants
citation: NPS Manzanar, 'Owens Valley Paiute'; NPS Manzanar Owens Valley Paiute page
quote: in 1863, forcibly removed 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon in the mountains south of Bakersfield
summary: NPS confirms the 1863 forced removal of about 1,000 Paiute to Fort Tejon and that many returned to the Owens Valley. The massacre of about 35 attributed to Capt. McLaughlin and the 380 remaining at Tejon in Jan. 1864 were not confirmed.

nations: Southern Cheyenne; Arapaho (Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes; Northern Cheyenne; Northern Arapaho)
citation: NPS Sand Creek Massacre NHS place page; Treaty of 1865 Art. VI; 12 Stat. 1163; 14 Stat. 703; Kappler II 887
quote: approximately 675 soldiers of the 1st and 3rd Regiments, Colorado Volunteer (U.S.) Cavalry, killed more than 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho over the course of seven hours
summary: About 675 men of the 1st and 3rd Colorado Cavalry under Col. John Chivington attacked Black Kettle's and White Antelope's camp, which flew a US flag, killing more than 230. Eleven months later the survivors ceded the Fort Wise reserve and their Colorado claims at the Little Arkansas, in a treaty that itself acknowledged the 'gross and wanton outrages'.

nations: Southern Cheyenne (Black Kettle's band); Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes
citation: NPS Washita Battlefield NHS, History & Culture; 15 Stat. 593; Kappler II 984-989
quote: approximately 30 to 60 Cheyenne and 20 cavalrymen lay dead in the snow and mud
summary: Custer's 7th Cavalry attacked Black Kettle's village on Nov. 27, 1868 in Sheridan's winter campaign; Black Kettle and his wife were killed; NPS gives 30 to 60 Cheyenne dead (other counts 13 to over 100) and 53 women and children taken captive. NPS says the loss of winter supplies forced many bands onto reservations. That the captives were held to compel surrender is interpretation; attribute it.

nations: Piikani (Piegan / Blackfeet), Heavy Runner's band; Blackfeet Nation
instrument: 25 Stat. 113 (confirmed as the 1888 agreement act); 18 Stat. 28 not checked
citation: Montana Historical Society (IEFA lesson; Henderson, Montana Magazine 2018) via search; 18 Stat. 28 [unchecked]; 25 Stat. 113
summary: Baker's 2nd Cavalry attacked Heavy Runner's Piikani camp on Jan. 23, 1870, not the band sought; the Army's count was 173 dead, mostly women, children and elders, and Henderson gives 217. Coordinates in the row (48.4,-111.1) are about 40 km east of the usually given site (about 48.39,-111.66, near the Marias in Toole/Pondera area). The 1873-74 reductions followed but no source here ties them to the massacre.

nations: Aravaipa and Pinal Apache (San Carlos Apache Tribe descendants)
instrument: Camp Grant reservation EO 1871-11-09; restored to public domain by EO 1872-12-14; San Carlos EO 1872-12-14
citation: HistoryNet; True West; Royce 1899 entry 541
quote: President restores to public domain reservation established at Camp Grant, Nov. 9, 1871.
summary: On Apr. 30, 1871 a Tucson party of Anglo-Americans, Mexican Americans and Tohono O'odham attacked Aravaipa and Pinal Apache families under Army protection, killing about 85 to 144, mostly women and children, and taking 27 to 30 children. A Camp Grant reserve was approved Nov. 9, 1871 and restored to the public domain Dec. 14, 1872 (Royce 541). The reserve was not a cession, and the massacre-to-reserve link is a sequence.

nations: Nimiipuu (Nez Perce), non-treaty bands (Joseph, Looking Glass, White Bird, Toohoolhoolzote)
citation: NPS Big Hole National Battlefield; 14 Stat. 647; Kappler II 843
quote: Between 60 and 90 nımí·pu· men, women, and children were killed during the battle
summary: Gibbon's troops and volunteers attacked the sleeping Nimiipuu camp at dawn on Aug. 9, 1877, killing 60 to 90 men, women and children; 31 soldiers and volunteers died (NPS). The "only about 30 were warriors" figure was not found in the NPS pages read. The bands were in flight after the 1877 order to move onto the reduced 1863 reservation.

nations: Mniconjou and Hunkpapa Lakota (Big Foot / Spotted Elk's band); Oglala Sioux Tribe, Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe descendants
instrument: 25 Stat. 888 (Act of Mar. 2, 1889, confirmed); 19 Stat. 254 (Act of Feb. 28, 1877; context)
citation: NPS, Wounded Knee National Historic Landmark nomination; 25 Stat. 888; 19 Stat. 254
quote: A total of at least 250 dead is almost certain.
summary: The 7th Cavalry killed at least 250 Lakota, mostly women, children and elders, while disarming Spotted Elk's band on Dec. 29, 1890; 146 were buried in the mass grave and Joseph Horn Cloud listed 186 dead (NHL nomination), with higher estimates near 300. The 350-375 figure was not verified. It came 21 months after the 1889 act and amid ration cuts; that is context, not a sourced cause of a land taking.

citation: General knowledge
summary: Spirit Lake (1857) was a killing of about 35 to 40 settlers by Inkpaduta's band, not a massacre of Native people; it followed the unpunished 1854 murder of Inkpaduta's brother Sintominaduta and family by Henry Lott. It was later invoked against all Dakota.

nations: Goshute (Skull Valley Band of Goshute; Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation)
citation: None found
summary: No specific massacre of Goshute people in Skull Valley could be verified in this pass. California Volunteers from Camp Douglas and Fort Ruby did kill Goshute in 1863 in western Utah/eastern Nevada before the Tooele Valley treaty, but specific sites were not confirmed.
reason_not_supported: No documented Skull Valley massacre was found. Do not map.

citation: NAHC Digital Atlas, Genocide MapServer service metadata (gis.cnra.ca.gov/arcgis/rest/services/NAHC/Genocide/MapServer); NAHC Genocide MapServer, layer 'An American Genocide'
quote: Recorded incidents in the California Genocide, 1846-1873, linked to timelines of incidents by region. Note: Locations as recorded in sources vary in precision.
summary: State-hosted ArcGIS layer of recorded incidents of the California genocide, 1846-1873, sourced from Madley's An American Genocide, with a note that location precision varies. NAHC also publishes regional genocide timelines (Sacramento Valley, Humboldt, Mendocino, etc.).

citation: Crossref record for Bales and Annerfalk (2024); Western Historical Quarterly 55(2):127-146 (2024), doi:10.1093/whq/whae002
quote: Introducing the Euro-Invasion Conflict Database 1513–1901
summary: Database of 1,375 conflicts between Indigenous peoples and colonizers/US forces, coded on up to 30 variables including coordinates and casualties, flagging 'genocidal massacres' using Madley's criteria. First compiled by Michael L. Nunnally, developed by the Rights Lab, University of Nottingham.

nations: Tolowa; Wiyot; Yurok; Hupa; Wailaki and others
citation: Northwestern California Genocide Project home page (nwgenocide.omeka.net); nwgenocide.omeka.net
quote: The Northwestern California Genocide Project is a Digital Archive put together and presented by Humboldt State University students.
summary: The project is a Humboldt State University student digital archive (Omeka) of items on genocidal events in northwestern California. It has browse, exhibit and map views of items, but no downloadable geodataset was seen. No license statement appears on the home page.

nations: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples (Australia; analog only)
citation: Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia 1788-1930, Introduction (University of Newcastle); c21ch.newcastle.edu.au/colonialmassacres/introduction.php
quote: The killing of an undefended group of six or more of them in one operation
summary: The project's introduction confirms the definition (six or more undefended people killed in one operation) and its method of grouping multi-site events and revising locations and estimates on review. The CC BY-NC 4.0 license and the deliberate offsetting of coordinates were not found on the introduction page.

citation: NPS unit pages (Sand Creek NHS, Washita NHS, Big Hole NB, Horseshoe Bend NMP); Wounded Knee NHL nomination
quote: the Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site was officially authorized on November 7, 2000
summary: NPS units for Sand Creek, Washita, Big Hole and Horseshoe Bend and the Wounded Knee NHL nomination exist and were read. Bear River NHL (1990) is confirmed only by secondary sources here. Public-domain status of NPS boundary GIS was not checked per dataset.

citation: Atlas derived layer (USFS Royce polygons) re-computed; cessions.json legal_type field; spherical-excess area
summary: By the dataset's legal_type field, 474 polygons (1,472M polygon-acres, 73.5%) are treaty_or_agreement, 76 statute (224M, 11.2%), 113 executive_order (198M, 9.9%) and 54 unknown (108M, 5.4%). Polygon acres overlap (sum 2,002M vs about 1,597M acres of union coverage on the repo's 0.1-degree grid), so these are shares of mapped polygon area, not of land.

nations: Western Shoshone; Goshute; Eastern and Western Apache; Paiute; Uintah Ute; Pima; Maricopa; Tohono O'odham (Papago); Yuma (Quechan); Walapai; Mohave; Hopi (Moki); Cocopah; Washoe; Methow; Okanagan; Chehalis; Chinook; Cowlitz
quote: No treaty of purchase was ever made with this tribe. The U.S. assumed title to their country
summary: Sixteen Royce areas (about 331M polygon-acres on recomputation) carry remarks that the United States took possession, assumed title, or that settlers took the land, without a treaty of purchase or relinquishment. Royce 473 (Washo) says the land was "taken possession of by settlers" without purchase by the U.S. Royce 682's remark says only "No treaty of purchase was ever made with these Indians"; the "assumed title" wording is in the next four remarks. 558 is a low-confidence number match.

nations: Apache; Walapai; Yuma; Mohave; Hopi; Cocopah; Pima; Maricopa; Papago
citation: Royce 1899 schedule p.922 and index; atlas cession-events.json; Royce 1899 p.922 (1886 Oct. entries); index (e.g., "MOHAVE, October 1, 1886")
quote: Country claimed by them at beginning of their relations with the U.S.
summary: The 1886-10-01 date comes from Royce's own schedule: the Southwest "country claimed" rows sit under the "1886 Oct." heading that follows the Pueblo grant confirmations (citing Stat. L. XI, 374), and Royce's index dates them October 1, 1886. The dataset's "statute" type comes from a link to a UGA eHistory "FedStatIndianLand" PDF for each area (e.g., 682c.pdf), not from any statute that ceded the land. Recomputed total for 682-689 is about 163M polygon-acres.

instrument: Royce Schedule pp. 780-784; atlas instrument ids TLA-U-CA-*
citation: Royce 1899 schedule pp.780-787; atlas layer; Royce 1899 p.782-783
quote: Cede all claim to territory outside of reserved tract
summary: Royce maps the 18 unratified 1851-52 California treaties as 35 polygons (about 88M polygon-acres), all typed "unknown". But Royce numbers 273-310 also include three non-California areas (289 Sioux 1851, 292 Minnesota 1830, 300 Fort Laramie 1851). No legal cession took place under the California treaties.

instrument: Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419 (July 8, 1852); Kappler IV 1081
citation: Kappler, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties vol. IV (1929), Unratified treaties, reprinting Senate Executive Journal; Kappler IV 1081-1085, citing Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419 (July 8, 1852)
quote: The eighteen treaties with Indian tribes in California received on the 7th and reported without amendment the 28th June, were severally read the second time
summary: Fillmore sent the 18 treaties to the Senate on June 1, 1852. The Senate received them June 7, the committee reported them without amendment June 28, and on July 8, 1852 the Senate unanimously refused consent to each treaty (Senate Executive Journal vol. 8, pp. 417-419). The injunction of secrecy was removed January 18, 1905 (NARA Prologue 2013, citing the Senate Executive Journal entry). Interior and the Indian Office recorded strong opposition among white Californians and in the California legislature and congressional delegation. The 'commissioner irregularities' reason is NARA's characterization. Acreage not checked here.

citation: Barker v. Harvey, 181 U.S. 481 (1901), quoting Act of Mar. 3, 1851, s.13; United States v. Title Ins. & Trust Co., 265 U.S. 472 (1924); 9 Stat. 631, s.13 (as quoted in 181 U.S. 481); 265 U.S. 472, 486
quote: all lands the claims to which shall not have been presented to the said commissioners within two years after the date of this act, shall be deemed, held and considered as part of the public domain of the United States
summary: The 1851 Act required private land claims in California to be presented to a commission within two years or be treated as abandoned. In Barker v. Harvey the Court held Mission Indians' occupancy rights forfeited because no claim was filed for them; in 1924 the Court refused to overrule Barker as a 'rule of property'.

nations: Indians of California; Mission Indians; Pit River
citation: Indian Claims Commission, Thompson et al. (Indians of California) v. United States, Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D, 347 consolidated: Findings of Fact (Part 1) and Final Determination; ICC Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D, 347 (consolidated), 13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 369, 543 (July 20, 1964); title phase 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 (1959)
quote: do have and recover of and from the defendant the net sum of $29,100,000
summary: The ICC entered a single compromise judgment of $29,100,000 (net) on July 20, 1964 in consolidated Dockets 31, 37, 80, 80-D and 347 (Indians of California, Mission Bands, Pit River). The ICC held Indian title in California was extinguished by the Act of March 3, 1851 (9 Stat. 631) and the Act of March 3, 1853 (10 Stat. 244), with taking and valuation as of March 3, 1853. The ICC put net acreage at about 64,425,000 acres, which gives roughly 45 cents an acre. Pit River objectors are recorded in the settlement findings. The 1964 appropriation and the 1972 refusal of checks were not checked.

instrument: Act of May 18, 1928, 45 Stat. 602; Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583 (1942), 102 Ct. Cl. 837 (1944)
citation: Indian Claims Commission, Thompson et al. v. United States, Opinion of the Commission (title), Dockets 31 and 37; 8 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, 31 (July 31, 1959), describing Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583 and 102 Ct. Cl. 837 (1944)
quote: the award was made on the basis of the value of the lands included in the 18 unratified treaties
summary: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 (45 Stat. 602), the Court of Claims gave the Indians of California a gross judgment of $17,058,941.98, reduced by offsets to a net recovery of about $5,000,000 (98 Ct. Cl. 583; 102 Ct. Cl. 837). The ICC later read that award as based on the value of the reserve lands promised in the 18 unratified treaties, not as payment for aboriginal title, and held that the Indians received no compensation for their aboriginal rights. The row's claim that the Court of Claims itself 'expressly said' it was not paying for a cession or taking is the ICC's later reading, not a quote from 102 Ct. Cl. 837.

citation: Treaty of Ruby Valley, Oct. 1, 1863 (Kappler II 851-853); Royce 1899 p.829; 18 Stat. 689, Arts. 2-4; Royce 1899 area 444
quote: No formal purchase of the territorial claim of these tribes or bands was made, but the U.S. took possession of the same
summary: The treaty defined Western Shoshone boundaries and granted passage, telegraph, stage, railroad and mining rights, but contains no land cession. Royce maps the area (444, about 75.7M polygon-acres) and says the U.S. 'took possession' without purchase. The dataset types it treaty_or_agreement because it links to Kappler.

citation: United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985); 470 U.S. 39, 41-42 (citing 11 Ind. Cl. Comm'n 387, 416 (1962); 40 Ind. Cl. Comm'n 318 (1977))
quote: the aboriginal title of the Western Shoshone had been extinguished in the latter part of the 19th century
summary: The ICC (1962) held Western Shoshone aboriginal title extinguished in the latter part of the 19th century and later (1977) awarded over $26 million; the Court of Claims affirmed in 1979. The "gradual encroachment by whites" wording, the July 1, 1872 valuation date and the 24.4M acre figure are from the ICC opinion, which was not reachable.

citation: United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985); 470 U.S. 39, 42
quote: this certification automatically appropriated the amount of the award and deposited it for the Tribe in an interest-bearing trust account
summary: The Court held that 'payment' occurred when the $26M award was certified and deposited in a Treasury trust account, barring the tribal-title defense, even though the Western Shoshone had not accepted the money. The Court relied on the government being both judgment debtor and trustee.

citation: CERD, Early Warning and Urgent Action Procedure, Decision 1 (68), United States of America (Western Shoshone); CERD/C/USA/DEC/1 (11 April 2006), paras. 3-4, 6, 10; Pub. L. 108-270, 118 Stat. 805 (July 7, 2004)
quote: The Committee has received credible information alleging that the Western Shoshone indigenous peoples are being denied their traditional rights to land
summary: At its 68th session (20 Feb to 10 Mar 2006) CERD acted on requests from the Western Shoshone National Council, Timbisha Shoshone, Winnemucca Indian Colony and Yomba Shoshone. It found credible information that Western Shoshone are being denied traditional land rights and that US measures may cumulatively cause irreparable harm. The US did reply (letter of 15 Feb 2006) but did not answer the list of issues or appear; CERD regretted that. CERD cited the IACHR Dann decision (Case 11.140, 27 Dec 2002) that the ICC process did not meet international norms, and urged a freeze on privatization and on grazing fees, trespass notices and impoundments. The Western Shoshone Claims Distribution Act (Pub. L. 108-270, July 7, 2004) provides for distribution of Docket 326-K funds; the $145-160M figure was not checked.

citation: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); Act of Feb. 28, 1877; 448 U.S. 371; 19 Stat. 254, ch. 72
quote: the court held that the Sioux were entitled to an award of interest on the principal sum of $17.1 million (the fair market value of the Black Hills as of 1877), dating from 1877
summary: Royce shows 598 (7.2M polygon-acres, Black Hills portion of the 1868 Great Sioux Reservation) and 597 (21.2M, art. 16 unceded territory) as cessions. In 1980 the Supreme Court affirmed that the 1877 Act was a taking under eminent domain, with interest on $17.1M from 1877 (about $106M in 1980). The Sioux refused payment; the fund is reported at over $1B.

citation: City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005); County of Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation, 470 U.S. 226 (1985); 544 U.S. 197, 221; 470 U.S. 226, 233-240
quote: evoke the doctrines of laches, acquiescence, and impossibility, and render inequitable the piecemeal shift in governance this suit seeks unilaterally to initiate
summary: Oneida II (1985) held the Oneidas had a federal common-law action for violation of possessory rights; the claim concerned New York's 1795 purchase, not the 1788 Fort Schuyler treaty. Sherrill (2005) barred the Nation from reviving sovereignty over parcels it repurchased, on laches, acquiescence and impossibility.

citation: Cayuga Indian Nation of New York v. Pataki, 413 F.3d 266 (2d Cir. June 28, 2005); 413 F.3d 266, 268-269, 273
quote: resulting in a total award of $247,911,999.42
summary: New York took 64,012 acres in 1795 and 3 more in 1807 under state treaties never ratified by the federal government. The district court awarded $247,911,999.42 (damages plus interest); the Second Circuit, applying Sherrill, held laches barred the possessory claim and entered judgment for defendants.

nations: Passamaquoddy; Penobscot; Houlton Band of Maliseet
citation: Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Pub. L. 96-420; 94 Stat. 1785
quote: There is hereby authorized to be appropriated $81,500,000
summary: Pub. L. 96-420 (94 Stat. 1785, Oct. 10, 1980) authorized $81.5M ($27M settlement fund, $54.5M land acquisition fund) and deemed prior transfers made "in accordance with the Constitution and all laws of the United States". The 12.5M acre claim size is not in the Act.

citation: Mashpee Tribe v. New Seabury Corp., 592 F.2d 575 (1st Cir. Feb. 13, 1979); Final Determination for Federal Acknowledgment of the Mashpee Wampanoag Indian Tribal Council, 72 Fed. Reg. 8007 (Feb. 22, 2007); 592 F.2d 575, 579-580; 72 FR 8007
quote: constitute an Indian tribe as of August 26, 1976: The date of the commencement of this law suit? No
summary: In a 40-day trial on tribal status (Oct. 1977 to Jan. 1978) the jury answered that the Mashpee were not a tribe on July 22, 1790, were a tribe on March 31, 1834 and March 3, 1842, and were not a tribe on June 23, 1869, May 28, 1870 or August 26, 1976. The First Circuit affirmed judgment for defendants. Interior's final determination acknowledging the Mashpee Wampanoag was published Feb. 22, 2007, effective May 23, 2007.

citation: Rhode Island Indian Claims Settlement Act, Pub. L. 95-395; 92 Stat. 813
quote: Rhode Island Indian Claims Settlement Fund into which $3,500,000 shall be deposited
summary: Pub. L. 95-395 (92 Stat. 813, Sept. 30, 1978) set a $3.5M fund and defined settlement lands as private settlement lands of about 900 acres plus public settlement lands; the common total of about 1,800 acres is consistent but not stated in the Act text checked.

nations: Kalapuya (Santiam, Tualatin, Yamhill etc.); Molalla; Clackamas
instrument: Unratified (NARA T494); successor: Treaty with the Kalapuya, etc., Jan. 22, 1855, 10 Stat. 1143
citation: NARA microfilm T494, Unratified Treaty File (UW Digital Collections list of titles); NARA T494, 'Documents relating to the negotiation of an unratified treaty of April 19, 1851, with the Kalapuya and Molala Indians'
quote: Documents relating to the negotiation of an unratified treaty of April 19, 1851, with the Kalapuya and Molala Indians
summary: The Willamette Valley Treaty Commission's 1851 treaties were never ratified; the T494 Unratified Treaty File holds at least one of them (April 19, 1851, Kalapuya and Molala). The other Champoeg treaties (Santiam, Tualatin, Yamhill, Luckiamute, Molala), Dart's advice and the 'effectively rejected through neglect' wording are from secondary sources (Oregon Encyclopedia; Lewis). The 1855 Kalapuya treaty (10 Stat. 1143) later ceded the valley.

citation: Oregon Organic Act, Aug. 14, 1848, s.1; Donation Land Claim Act, Sept. 27, 1850; 9 Stat. 323, s.1; 9 Stat. 496, ch. 76
quote: so long as such rights shall remain unextinguished by treaty between the United States and such Indians
summary: The 1848 Organic Act protected Indian rights to land so long as they remained unextinguished by treaty. The 1850 Donation Act nonetheless granted free land to white settlers before any ratified cession in western Oregon; Delegate Thurston had called extinguishment of Native title the 'first prerequisite step'.

nations: Chinook; Clatsop; Waukikum; Chehalis; Cowlitz; Klikitat
instrument: Tansey Point treaties of Aug. 1851 (Anson Dart), unratified
citation: Royce 1899 schedule p.833; Royce 1899 area 458
quote: without any treaty. assigning to the Indians first only one small reserve
summary: Royce 458 (4.9M polygon-acres) is recorded as taken without any treaty, with only the Chehalis reserve assigned; the dataset dates it 1864-07-08 and types it executive_order. Tansey Point treaties were unratified (secondary; not checked here).

citation: Royce 1899 schedule p.812; Royce 1899 area 397
quote: The treaties were not ratified, but the U.S. authorities assumed that the cession was binding, and by Executive order of Noy. 9, 1855
summary: Royce 397 (3.9M polygon-acres) is the unratified 1855 Oregon coast treaty area; Royce says the U.S. treated the cession as binding anyway, and the Coast (Siletz) reservation was set apart inside it by executive order of Nov. 9, 1855.

nations: Comanche; Caddo; Anadahko; Waco; Tonkawa; Lipan Apache; Wichita and others
citation: Joint Resolution for annexing Texas, Mar. 1, 1845, as quoted in Texas Ordinance of July 4, 1845; atlas grid; 5 Stat. 797; repo grid recomputation
quote: shall also retain all the vacant and unappropriated lands lying within its limits
summary: Texas kept its public lands at annexation (5 Stat. 797). Five Royce polygons touch Texas (478, 511, 512, 513, 688). The central Texas box (94-103W, 28-33N) is about 45% covered on the repo grid, but mostly by Royce 478 (Kiowa-Comanche, about 41% of the box), not Apache 688 (about 11%). The 1854 twelve-league reserves and 1859 removal were not checked against Texas statutes.

citation: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Pub. L. 92-203; Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955); 85 Stat. 688, s.4; 348 U.S. 272
quote: including any aboriginal hunting or fishing rights that may exist, are hereby extinguished
summary: ANCSA extinguished all aboriginal title and claims in Alaska. Its fund was $462.5M from the Treasury plus $500M in revenue sharing ($962.5M). Land grants in the Act text are about 40M acres (22M village, 16M regional remainder of 38M, 2M other); 44-45M is a later conveyance figure. Tee-Hit-Ton held "the taking by the United States of unrecognized Indian title is not compensable under the Fifth Amendment".

citation: Apology Resolution, Pub. L. 103-150; Newlands Resolution; 107 Stat. 1510 (preamble); 30 Stat. 750
quote: never directly relinquished their claims to their inherent sovereignty as a people or over their national lands to the United States
summary: After the 1893 overthrow, the Republic of Hawaii ceded about 1.8M acres of crown, government and public lands to the US by the 1898 Newlands Resolution, without Native Hawaiian consent or compensation. Congress in 1993 found Native Hawaiians never directly relinquished their claims.

citation: Mountain States Tel. & Tel. Co. v. Pueblo of Santa Ana, 472 U.S. 237 (1985), quoting S. Rep. No. 492, 68th Cong. 1st Sess. (1924); 472 U.S. 237, 243-244
quote: there are now approximately 3,000 claimants to lands within the exterior boundaries of the Pueblo grants. The non-Indian claimants with their families comprise about 12,000 per- sons
summary: The 3,000 claimants / 12,000 persons figures are confirmed (S. Rep. 492 quoted in 472 U.S. 237). The phrase "moral, if not legal, obligation to make reasonable restitution" does not appear in 472 U.S. 237; its source is unverified.

citation: Royce 1899 Schedule, area 687; Treaty with Mexico (Gadsden), Dec. 30, 1853; ICC Final Report (1978) docket table; Royce 1899 area 687; 10 Stat. 1031; ICC Docket 345, 19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 394 (1968) (title); Dockets 102 and 345, 38 Ind. Cl. Comm. 542, 559 (July 21, 1976)
quote: No treaty of purchase was ever made with these tribes, who have a common
summary: The US acquired the area from Mexico by the Gadsden treaty (10 Stat. 1031), with no O'odham party. Royce 687 says no treaty of purchase was ever made with these tribes and the US took possession. The ICC found Papago title in Docket 345 (19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 394, Sept. 10, 1968) and entered a $26,000,000 compromise award in Dockets 102 and 345 on July 21, 1976.

nations: Wampanoag; Narragansett; Pequot; Mohegan; Lenape; Powhatan; Piscataway; Catawba; Abenaki and others
instrument: (none in federal record) colonial deeds, conquest, colonial and state statutes
citation: Atlas grid recomputation; cession-cells.json
summary: Royce covers federal-era cessions only. On the repo's 0.1-degree grid, test boxes over New England (69-73.5W, 41.5-45N), Maryland-Delaware-New Jersey and the Virginia Piedmont have 0% Royce coverage. Overall, Royce union coverage is about 1,597M acres against about 1,894M acres of contiguous-US land, so roughly 300M acres (about 16%) of the lower 48 has no Royce polygon at all, before adding Alaska and Hawaii.

instrument: Map 'Indian Land Areas Judicially Established' (USGS for ICC), 1:4,000,000, Albers
citation: Indian Claims Commission Final Report (1978), Fiscal Year Totals of Dockets Completed and Awards; Esri FeatureServer metadata; ICC Final Report (1978) p. 125 table; Esri FeatureServer layer 5
summary: The ICC Final Report's table shows 204 dockets completed by dismissal and 342 by award (546 total) through Sept. 30, 1978, with cumulative awards of $818,172,606.64. A public Esri FeatureServer exists with layer 5 'Indian Land Areas Judicially Established 1978', described as areas where a tribe proved original occupancy before the ICC or Court of Claims.

instrument: Executive orders and acts restoring reservation land to the public domain
citation: Royce 1899 schedule (699, 717, White Mountain entries); Royce 1899 pp.930, 944
summary: Crosswalk status=taken areas are mostly restorations to public domain. 699 followed the 1889 Sioux Act, which took effect only on Sioux assent (proclaimed Feb. 10, 1890), so it is a ratified cession, not a unilateral taking. 717 (Colville north half, 1892) was without tribal consent.

nations: Sac and Fox; Choctaw; Chickasaw; Wichita; Crow; Ute; Jicarilla Apache
quote: The Crow refused to remove to the reserve and Congress failed to ratify the agreement.
summary: Several reserves were set apart by executive order under agreements Congress never ratified: 557 Judith Basin (Crow, 1874), 563 Jicarilla (1874), 609 San Juan (Southern Ute, 1878 agreement), 540a Wichita (1872 agreement). Royce 368 (7.1M) was a lease, not a cession, until 1866.

citation: treaty-land-atlas crosswalk royce-entry-roles.csv (recomputed); repo crosswalk
summary: The crosswalk has 1,172 role rows over 724 Royce area ids. Distinct areas per role: reserved 469, confirmed 51, described_or_recognized 36, retroceded 57, us_reserved 4, ceded 402, ceded_part 16, other 62. 498 areas carry at least one promise role (reserved/confirmed/described_or_recognized).

citation: treaty-land-atlas crosswalk royce-entry-roles.csv (recomputed); repo crosswalk
summary: Of 498 areas with a promise role, the crosswalk gives 257 ceded and 2 taken (259), 227 kept and 12 unclear. Acreage sums were not recomputed. At least one "kept" promise area is mislabeled: Royce 516 is the 1868 relinquishment of Sioux land outside the Great Sioux Reservation, a cession, not a reserve. "Kept" means kept as of Royce (to 1894) only.

citation: General Allotment Act; Collier 1934 figures as reported; 24 Stat. 388
summary: Royce ends in 1894, so "kept" predates most allotment and surplus-land openings. The 138 million acres (1887) to 48 million (1934) figures are John Collier's 1934 figures as repeated by secondary sources; the 1928 Meriam Report cannot be their source. A 1938 Interior Department report is quoted with 130 million (1887) and 49 million (1933). Say "roughly 90 million acres left Indian hands 1887-1934 (Collier, 1934)". Royce 700-705, 715 and 374 are "kept" in the crosswalk; 540 (Wind River) is "unclear", not "kept".

nations: Sioux (Dakota/Lakota); Cheyenne; Arapaho; Crow; Assiniboine; Gros Ventre (Hidatsa); Mandan; Arikara
instrument: Kappler II 440-442 (1903 ed.) = 594 (1904 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 prints only an explanatory note, not the treaty
citation: Kappler, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties, vol. II (1903 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 note; Kappler II 440-442 (1903 ed.; p. 594 in 1904 ed.), Art. 5; 11 Stat. 749
quote: It is however, understood that, m making this recognition and acknowledgement, the aforesaid Indian nations do not hereby abandon
summary: Article 5 defines by metes and bounds the territory of each nation; the nations did not abandon claims to other lands. The repo maps these as 'described_or_recognized' but only in fragments: there is no single polygon per nation, and area 300 is labelled 'several nations' at only 6.3 million acres.

nations: Blackfeet (Blackfoot Confederacy: Piegan, Blood, Siksika); Gros Ventre (A'aninin)
citation: Blackfoot treaty Oct. 17, 1855; Royce 1899 Schedule; 11 Stat. 657, Art. 3; Royce 1899 p. 855 (remarks)
quote: shall be a common hunting-ground for ninety-nine years
summary: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5 described a Blackfoot territory; whether any Blackfeet attended or signed was not checked (Kappler does not print the signatures). The 1855 treaty recognized Blackfoot territory and made a large tract a common hunting ground for 99 years. A treaty of Sept. 1, 1868 that would have reduced it was never ratified; per Royce the Executive order of July 5, 1873 (and later orders, the 1874 act and the 1888 agreement) cut it down.

citation: Royce 1899 Schedule; Crow treaty May 7, 1868; Royce 1899 p. 849 area 517; 15 Stat. 649
quote: This relinquishment comprises that portion of the country assigned them by unratified Fort Laramie treaty of Sept. 17, 1851, not included within the
summary: Crow country recognized in 1851 (30.1 million acres in repo polygon 517) was relinquished outside an 1868 reservation, which was then cut in 1880-82 (619) and 1891 (714), leaving 715.

instrument: Fort Laramie 1851; EO Apr. 12, 1870; EO July 13, 1880; act Mar. 3, 1891
citation: Royce 1899 Schedule; Royce 1899 p. 787 area 529
quote: comprised part of their recognized territory by the Fort Laramie treaty of 1851, the remainder of that tract being considered as ceded
summary: The 1851 territory of the Three Affiliated Tribes outside the 1870 executive-order Fort Berthold reserve was 'considered as ceded' with no cession instrument (529). The 1880 order removed more (620).

citation: Fort Laramie treaty Apr. 29, 1868, Art. 2; 15 Stat. 635, 636, Art. 2
quote: set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the Indians herein named
summary: Art. 2 set apart, for the absolute and undisturbed use of the Sioux, the land from the low-water mark on the Missouri's east bank west to the 104th meridian, between the 46th parallel and the Nebraska line, plus all existing reservations on the east bank. Royce 516 is not this reservation: Royce p. 849 numbers 516 as the 1868 cession of Sioux land outside it.

citation: Royce 1899 Schedule, remark for area 516; Royce 1899 p. 849 area 516
quote: This cession comprises that portion of the Sioux territory assigned them by Fort
summary: Repo maps the Great Sioux Reservation as Royce 516 (status kept), but polygon 516 covers only about 4.3 million acres and its own note doubts the match. The union of 598 (Black Hills cession) + 699 (1889 restored remainder) + 700-705 (six 1889 reservations) is about 27.7 million acres, which fits the Art. 2 area.

citation: Fort Laramie 1868 Art. 16; Royce 1899 Schedule; 15 Stat. 635, Art. 16 and Art. 11; 19 Stat. 254; Royce 1899 p. 849 areas 584, 597
quote: Horn mountains shall be held and considered to be unceded Indian
summary: Art. 16 kept the country north of the North Platte and east of the Big Horn summits as 'unceded Indian territory' closed to whites; Art. 11 kept hunting on the Republican Fork. These were extinguished by the 1875 agreement (584) and the 1876-77 Black Hills agreement/act (597).

citation: Medicine Lodge treaty Art. 12; Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock; 15 Stat. 581, Art. 12; 187 U.S. 553 (1903)
quote: Four hundred and fifty-six male adults therefore constituted more than three fourths of the certified number
summary: The 1865 reserve was cut in 1867 to the Medicine Lodge reservation; Art. 12 required three-fourths of adult men to sign any cession. The Jerome commission certified 456 signers out of 562 adult men, which it counted as more than three-fourths; the tribes said their assent was obtained by misrepresentation and that three-fourths had not assented. Congress ratified a changed agreement in 1900 and Lone Wolf upheld Congress's power to do so. The three-fourths shortfall is the tribes' allegation, not a finding.

citation: Medicine Lodge (Cheyenne-Arapaho) Oct. 28, 1867; Act of Mar. 3, 1891 sec. 13; 15 Stat. 593; 26 Stat. 989, 1022, sec. 13
quote: The said Cheyenne and Arapahoe tribes of Indians hereby cede
summary: The 1867 treaty reservation lay in the Cherokee Outlet; the nations never settled there and an 1869 executive order substituted a reserve on the North Canadian and Washita (525, 4.3 million acres), which was ceded subject to allotment in 1891.

citation: Fort Wise Feb. 18, 1861; Little Arkansas Oct. 14, 1865 and Senate amendment; 12 Stat. 1163; 14 Stat. 703, 707-708 (amendment 1)
quote: shall designate for said tribes a reservation, no part of which shall be within the State of Kansas
summary: Fort Wise ceded most of the 1851 territory and reserved a tract between the Sandy Fork and the Arkansas. The 1865 treaty ceded that reserve and set apart a new one between the Arkansas and Cimarron (partly in Kansas). The Senate amended it on May 22, 1866 so that no part could be in Kansas or on other tribes' land without consent; the chiefs assented Nov. 10 and 19, 1866, and no such reservation was ever designated. The Senate also struck the words naming Col. J. M. Chivington from Art. 6.

nations: Ute (Tabeguache/Uncompahgre, Muache, Capote, Weeminuche, Yampa, Grand River, Uintah bands)
citation: Ute treaty Mar. 2, 1868 Art. 2; Act of June 15, 1880; 15 Stat. 619, Art. 2; 21 Stat. 199, ch. 223
quote: fifteen miles due north of where said meridian
summary: Art. 2 reserved Colorado west of the 107th meridian and south of a line 15 miles north of the 40th parallel (566+616+617, about 16 million acres in repo polygons). Brunot (1873) took the San Juan strip (566); after the 1879 Meeker events the 1880 act removed White River and Uncompahgre Utes, leaving the Southern Ute strip (617).

instrument: 18 Stat. 685 (1863, per Kappler margin); 15 Stat. 673 (1868); 18 Stat. 291 (1874 act ratifying 1872 agreement); 33 Stat. 1016 (1905)
citation: Fort Bridger 1863 and 1868; Act of Mar. 3, 1905; Wyoming v. EPA; Kappler II 648-650 (1903 ed.); 18 Stat. 685; 15 Stat. 673; 33 Stat. 1016; 875 F.3d 505
quote: Congress evinced a clear intent to diminish the Reservation
summary: The 1863 treaty recognized about 44 million acres of Shoshone country; the 1868 treaty reserved about 3 million (539+540 = 3.2 million acres in repo). The southern part was ceded in 1872 (539). The 1905 act opened land north of the Big Wind River; in 2017 the Tenth Circuit held that act diminished the reservation (Riverton outside).

citation: Andrew Jackson, Letter to the Creek Indians, Mar. 23, 1829 (Papers of Andrew Jackson vol. VII, via American Presidency Project); Jackson to Creeks, Mar. 23, 1829
quote: as long as the grass grows or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours for ever.
summary: Jackson told the Creeks the western land would be theirs 'as long as the grass grows or the water runs'. This is a presidential promise, not treaty text; the binding guarantees are in the Removal Act sec. 3 and the removal treaties.

citation: Creek treaties 1832 and 1833; Creek treaty 1866; 7 Stat. 366; 7 Stat. 417, preamble and Art. III; 14 Stat. 785, Art. 3
quote: secure a country and permanent home to the whole Creek nation of Indians
summary: The 1833 treaty (7 Stat. 417) promised "a country and permanent home to the whole Creek nation" and in Art. III a patent in fee simple "so long as they shall exist as a nation, and continue to occupy the country". The 1866 treaty ceded the west half of the domain. McGirt held the reservation was never disestablished.

citation: Cherokee treaties 1833, 1835, 1866; Act of Mar. 3, 1893; 7 Stat. 414; 7 Stat. 478, Arts. 2 and 5; 14 Stat. 799, Art. 17; 27 Stat. 612, 640
quote: future time without their consent, be included within the territorial
summary: New Echota (1835) confirmed 7 million acres plus a perpetual outlet west and promised the land would never, without Cherokee consent, be put within any state or territory. The 1866 treaty ceded the Neutral Land in trust for sale; the Outlet was sold under the 1893 act. The 1838 patent wording ("revert... extinct or abandon") was not found in any source available here.

citation: Dancing Rabbit Creek 1830; Choctaw-Chickasaw treaties 1855 and 1866; 7 Stat. 333, Art. 2; 11 Stat. 611, Art. 9; 14 Stat. 769, Art. 3
quote: sum of three hundred thousand dollars, hereby cede to the United States
summary: The words "in fee simple to them and their descendants" are in the 1830 Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty, Art. 2 (7 Stat. 333), not the 1842 patent. The 1855 treaty leased the land west of the 98th meridian to the United States, and the 1866 treaty ceded that Leased District for $300,000. Where the $300,000 went is not stated in these sources; drop "went largely to the Kiowa-Comanche and Wichita".

nations: Wyandot; Delaware; Shawnee; Ottawa; Chippewa; Potawatomi; Miami; Eel River; Wea; Kickapoo; Piankashaw; Kaskaskia
citation: Treaty of Greenville, Aug. 3, 1795, Art. 5; 7 Stat. 49, Art. 5
quote: have a right to those lands, are quietly to enjoy them, hunting, planting, and dwelling thereon
summary: Art. 4 relinquished US claims to Indian lands north and west of the Greenville line, and Art. 5 says the tribes 'are quietly to enjoy them'. That promised zone has no polygon of its own in the repo; it appears only as later cessions (1803-1840s).

citation: Hellgate treaty July 16, 1855, Art. 11; Flathead act Apr. 23, 1904; 12 Stat. 975, Art. 11; 33 Stat. 302, ch. 1495
quote: above the Loo-lo fork, shall be carefully surveyed and examined
summary: Art. 11 provided that the Bitterroot Valley above the Lolo fork would be surveyed and examined before deciding whether it would be the Salish reservation. The 1904 act opened the Jocko (Flathead) reservation. summary: On June 23, 1852 the Senate struck Art. 3 of each treaty (the reserve of about ten miles on each side of the Minnesota River) and substituted ten cents an acre plus tracts to be chosen by the President. The bands assented on Sept. 8, 1852 (Traverse des Sioux) and Sept. 4, 1852 (Mendota). quote: it appeared that 41 signatures of chiefs, including 6 out of the 8 sachems of the nation, had been affixed to the treaty
summary: The Senate amended the treaty (June 11, 1838) and required each tribe to assent in council. Van Buren reported only 16 Seneca chiefs signed in council and 41 signatures in all, against 74 to 80 or more chiefs; he said the condition had not been met and that improper means had been used, and a Senate committee found bribery clearly shown in at least one case. The Senate ratified anyway and the treaty was proclaimed Apr. 4, 1840. The Society of Friends' 1840 Case of the Seneca Indians counts 16, later 31, of 81 chiefs. The quoted "forty-two out of eighty-one" was not found.

summary: The Senate added a clause that the treaty admitted no greater Indian title than existed under Mexican law (Box Elder new Art. 5; Fort Bridger Art. 7).
